    Content from Digital lives: why we protect data and systems

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How have digital networks changed life for individuals, groups and organisations?
    • Why do we protect data and systems, and what happens when we fail?
    • Why do attackers so often target people instead of technology?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • describe how digital networks have changed everyday life for individuals, groups and organisations (ULO 1)
    • explain why we protect data and systems, using confidentiality, integrity and availability (ULO 1)
    • describe how a successful attack affects people at the individual, group and organisational level (ULO 1)

    This episode matches Week 1 of The Human Firewall microcredential. The second half of the week is in the next episode, Social engineering: hacking the human.

    Your digital life

    Think about yesterday. Your phone woke you up. You may have checked messages before getting out of bed, tapped a card or a watch to pay for coffee, caught a bus with a travel card, or logged in to a learning site. Perhaps you booked a doctor’s appointment online or ordered dinner through an app.

    Every one of those steps sent information somewhere: your name, your location, your payment details, the time. It travelled across networks to companies you may never think about. Most of the time that is fine, and it is why life is so convenient. The point is to notice how much of your life now sits on other people’s systems.

    McAfee and Brynjolfsson (2018) argue that three changes are happening together: smarter machines doing work that people used to do, online platforms where many people and businesses meet, and the crowd of people who contribute information and ideas online. You do not need the whole book to use their main point. Digital technology now shapes how people, groups and organisations work, so a weakness in it can reach all three.

    Three levels

    We will look at the effect of digital networks at three levels. You will use them again and again in this course.

    Level What networks gave What networks cost
    Individuals Speed and convenience. You can bank at midnight, in your pyjamas. You hand over more personal information than people did a generation ago, to more organisations, and you often cannot see where it ends up.
    Groups, such as families, sports clubs and friendship circles Easy contact. Everyone stays in touch. A single careless post can reveal things about everybody in the group.
    Organisations They can serve thousands of customers at once. They now depend on those networks. If systems go down or data leaks, the business can stop and customers lose trust.

    Why do we protect data and systems?

    Security people usually give three reasons. You can think of them as three promises.

    • Confidentiality: information is seen only by the people who should see it.
    • Integrity: information is accurate and has not been changed by someone who should not change it.
    • Availability: the information and systems are there when you need them.

    Break any one promise and real people are affected. A leaked medical record breaks confidentiality. A bank balance altered by a criminal breaks integrity. A hospital that cannot open its patient files breaks availability.

    Why attackers go for people

    Imagine a house with a strong front door, three locks and an alarm, and an owner who will open the door for anyone who sounds confident and in a hurry. A burglar would not bother with the locks.

    Attackers have noticed that the easiest way into a digital system is often not the system at all. It is the person using it. Tricking people into giving up information, access or money is called social engineering, and the next episode covers it in detail. For now, hold on to this idea: technology protects data, but people use the technology, so people are part of the defence.

    What it costs when an attack works

    We use the same three levels to look at the harm.

    • Individuals. Money lost, accounts taken over, and stress. Identity theft is when someone uses your personal details, such as your name and date of birth, to pretend to be you. Fixing it can take months. The harm is not only financial. People often feel embarrassed, and embarrassment stops them from reporting.
    • Groups. One person’s compromised account can be used to attack their contacts, because a message from a friend or colleague is trusted. A group’s trust in each other can also be damaged.
    • Organisations. Money, lost work time, legal and regulatory action, and a damaged reputation. Customers whose information is exposed often become targets for further scams, because criminals can use real details to sound convincing.

    These levels connect. An individual falls for a message, that gives the attacker access to the organisation, and the organisation’s customers pay the price. When you analyse an incident, separate the people hurt first from the people hurt later.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Follow the harm (5 minutes)

    A fictional scenario. Priya works at a small physiotherapy clinic. An email arrives that looks as if it is from the clinic owner. It says: “I’m in a meeting. Buy five gift cards right now and send me the codes. I’ll explain later.” Priya buys the cards with her own money and sends the codes. The email was from an attacker.

    Write one or two sentences for each level: individual, group and organisation. For each, say who is hurt, how, and whether they are hurt first or later. Then name one promise (confidentiality, integrity or availability) that might also be broken if the attacker went further.

    One worked answer. Yours may differ.

    • Individual: Priya loses her own money, and she may feel embarrassed and delay telling anyone. She is hurt first.
    • Group: if the attacker reached her mailbox, her colleagues could be targeted next. They are hurt later.
    • Organisation: the clinic loses time dealing with the incident, and its owner’s name has been used to deceive staff. Patients could be hurt later if the attacker used what they learned for more scams.
    • Promise: if the attacker gained access to patient emails, confidentiality would be broken. If they changed appointment records, integrity would be.
    Challenge

    Challenge: How has one everyday task changed in 50 years? (20 minutes)

    Digital networks are part of almost every everyday task. When a task moves online, three things change: who you deal with, what information you hand over, and where that information goes.

    Pick one everyday task and compare how it was done about 50 years ago with how it is done now. Choose one of these, or pick your own:

    • banking (paying a bill or checking your balance)
    • booking a doctor’s appointment
    • finding a job
    • buying a train or bus ticket

    1. Choose your task (1 minute).

    2. Describe “then” (3 minutes). Use the notes below. You do not need exact dates. As an optional extra, ask an older relative or neighbour how they did it.

    3. Describe “now” (3 minutes). Think about the last time you did the task yourself and write down each step.

    4. Fill in a table (8 minutes) with these three rows and two columns, “Then” and “Now”. Use one or two short sentences in each cell.

      Then (about 50 years ago) Now
      Who did you deal with?
      What information did you hand over?
      Where did that information go?

    5. Write 3 to 4 sentences (5 minutes) answering: What got easier? What new risk appeared, and who could take advantage of it?

    Do not use anyone’s real name or private details. Describe your own experience, or a general experience of “an older person”.

    Notes on “then”. These describe the usual way, not exact dates.

    Task How it was usually done about 50 years ago
    Banking Visit a branch in business hours with a passbook or cheque book. A teller recorded your transaction by hand or on a branch machine. Paper statements came by post.
    Booking a doctor Phone or visit the surgery. A receptionist wrote it in an appointment book. Your records were kept on paper in the surgery.
    Finding a job Read newspaper advertisements, ask people you knew, or visit an employment office. You posted or handed in a paper application.
    Buying a ticket Queue at the station window and pay in cash. A staff member issued a paper ticket.

    This worked answer uses booking a doctor’s appointment. Your task may be different. Check that your answers have the same kind of detail.

    Then (about 50 years ago) Now
    Who did you deal with? Usually one person: the receptionist, by phone or in person at the surgery. The receptionist, but also an online booking company or app, the clinic’s software supplier, and possibly a text-message service.
    What information did you hand over? Your name, a phone number or address, and a short reason. Most of it was spoken or written on paper. Your name, date of birth, mobile number, email and Medicare number. You may also tick the reason for the visit and agree to terms you did not read in full.
    Where did that information go? A paper diary and a filing cabinet at the clinic, kept in one building. A company’s database, possibly in a cloud service in another place or country, shared across several systems, and sometimes copied to your phone’s apps.

    Short answer: Booking is now faster and I can do it at any hour without queuing. But more companies now hold my details, and I cannot see where they are stored. An attacker no longer needs to break into one filing cabinet. They only need to trick one person or one company, for example by sending a fake text that looks like a booking reminder and asks me to “confirm my details”. Because the information is held in many places, a problem with any one of them can affect me.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Comparing technology instead of the task. “Then there were no phones” does not answer the question. Describe who you dealt with and what you handed over.
    • Leaving out where the information goes. “It’s online” is not an answer. Say where it is kept and who else can see it.
    • Only listing good things. Say what got easier, but also name one new risk.
    • Guessing exact dates or numbers. Use “usually” and “typically”. Do not invent facts.
    • Naming real people. Keep family stories general, with no names or private details.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Dr Okafor’s clinic is hit by an attack, and for two days staff cannot open any patient files. Which of the three promises of security has been broken?

      • A. Confidentiality
      • B. Integrity
      • C. Availability
      • D. None. No information was leaked, so no promise was broken.

    2. Mia posts a photo from her netball team’s trip, with the players’ names and the hotel’s name in the caption. Which level of impact does this show most clearly?

      • A. Individual only, because Mia took the photo.
      • B. Group, because one post can reveal things about everybody in the group.
      • C. Organisation, because netball clubs are businesses.
      • D. None, because the photo is not private.
    1. C. Availability means information and systems are there when you need them. Nothing was leaked or changed, but staff could not use the files, and patients are affected. Option D is wrong because availability is one of the three promises, even when nothing is stolen.
    2. B. A single careless post can reveal things about everyone in the group, such as who is travelling together and where they are staying. Option A misses the other players, option C confuses a club with a business, and option D forgets that a public caption can be read by anyone.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one or two prompts and write 3 to 6 sentences for each. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords.

    • Your digital life. How much of your own day depends on digital networks? Think of one ordinary day and list the apps, devices and online services you used. How do you think life was different for people 50 years ago?
    • If it all failed. Imagine the networks you rely on stopped working for a week. What would happen in your life and in your community? Who might want to make a network fail, and why? Use only well-documented real examples, not rumours.

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes (read aloud in sections, or ask learners to read it first). Exercises 35 minutes: Follow the harm 5, then-and-now challenge 20, quick check 5, discussion 5. The optional interview with a relative is homework, not class time.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners compare technology (“no phones then”) instead of the task. Ask “who did you deal with?” to pull them back.
    • Learners think security only means keeping secrets. Use the hospital example to show that availability and integrity matter as much as confidentiality.
    • Learners assume attackers need technical skill. Leave the answer for episode 2, but plant the question here.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share (see the general notes). The “if it all failed” prompt works well with a short whole-room list of what each pair would lose first.

    Tip. Collect the “new risks” from the then-and-now challenge on a board.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Learn the basics gives plain-language advice on staying safe online.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 1 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • Digital networks bring speed and convenience, and they also spread our information across more organisations than before.
    • Look at impact on three levels: individuals, groups and organisations.
    • We protect data and systems to keep three promises: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
    • Attackers often target the person using a system, because it is easier than breaking the technology.
    • The harm from an attack spreads, so separate the people hurt first from the people hurt later.

    References

    McAfee, A. and Brynjolfsson, E. (2018) Machine, platform, crowd: harnessing our digital future. New York: W.W. Norton.

    Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Learn the basics. Available at: https://www.cyber.gov.au/learn-basics (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Social engineering: hacking the human

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is social engineering, and why does it work on sensible people?
    • What are the main tactics, and how do you tell them apart?
    • How does an attack unfold, and what helps you stop one?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • name the main social-engineering tactics (phishing, pretexting, baiting, tailgating, quid pro quo) and explain why they work on people (ULO 1)
    • recognise a social-engineering attempt in a short scenario and name the tactic used (ULO 1)
    • describe the four stages of an attack and the habits that disrupt it (ULO 1)

    This episode matches Week 1 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Digital lives, which explains why attackers go for people. Here we look at how.

    What is social engineering?

    Social engineering means tricking people into giving up information, access or money, by attacking their trust, habits and emotions instead of the technology. It works because people are helpful, polite, busy and sometimes frightened. Those are good human qualities. Attackers turn them into weaknesses.

    Six levers

    Attackers use a handful of levers again and again.

    Lever What it sounds like
    Authority The message seems to come from your boss, a bank or the police.
    Urgency You must act now, or something bad will happen.
    Fear Your account will be closed.
    Helpfulness Could you hold the door? I have forgotten my pass.
    Curiosity What is in this file labelled “salaries”?
    Reward You have won a prize, or you can get a refund.

    Attackers often combine levers. If a message pushes one of them hard, slow down. The feeling of being rushed is itself a warning sign.

    The main tactics

    You will meet each of these in the challenges below.

    • Phishing is a fake message, usually an email, designed to look as if it comes from someone you trust. It tries to get you to click a link, open a file or hand over details. It is sent to many people at once, hoping a few respond. When the message is aimed at one person or organisation and customised with real details, it is called spear phishing. Scam texts are sometimes called smishing, and scam phone calls vishing.
    • Pretexting means inventing a believable story, the pretext, to get information. A caller says, “I’m from the IT help desk, and I need to confirm your username to fix a fault.” There is no fault. The story is the whole attack. Good pretexters do their homework, so they know names, job titles and workplace jargon.
    • Baiting offers something tempting. The classic example is a USB drive left in a car park and labelled “Wages 2026”. Curiosity wins, someone plugs it in, and malicious software gets onto the computer. Baiting can be digital too, such as a free film download that carries malware.
    • Tailgating, or piggybacking, is the physical one. Someone follows you through a secure door because you were polite and held it open. They may carry a box, wear a lanyard, or simply look as if they belong.
    • Quid pro quo is Latin for “something for something”. The attacker offers a service or favour in return for information or access, such as free technical support that starts with your password.

    There are other tactics, but if you can recognise these five you can recognise most of what you will meet.

    How an attack unfolds

    Most attacks are not one trick. They follow four stages.

    1. Research. The attacker collects information about you or your organisation from social media, a company website, a staff directory or an earlier data breach. This stage is quiet. You will never see it happen.
    2. Building trust. The attacker makes contact and creates a believable reason to be there: the pretext, the fake logo, the confident voice.
    3. The exploit. The attacker asks for what they actually want: a password, a payment, a door held open, a file opened.
    4. The exit. The attacker covers their tracks or disappears. Often the victim does not realise anything has happened for days or weeks.

    Small facts feel like proof (“she knew my manager’s name”), but anyone can gather them.

    What helps

    These skills are learnable, and you do not need to be technical.

    • Slow down. If a message creates pressure, pause. Real banks and real bosses can wait five minutes.
    • Check by a different route. Do not use the phone number or link in the message. Look up the real number yourself, open the official app, or walk over and ask the colleague.
    • Report it. Telling someone quickly limits the damage, and a fast report is a good outcome, not a failure. Organisations that blame people teach them to stay quiet. Organisations that thank people for reporting find problems sooner.

    Technology helps too. A second step when you log in, called multi-factor authentication, means a stolen password alone is not enough. The National Cyber Security Centre (2024) makes a related point for organisations: they should use several layers of defence and should not depend mainly on staff spotting every phishing message. But technology never covers everything, which is why this course is about people.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Spot the phish (10 minutes)

    Social engineering works because it looks ordinary. First practise spotting fake messages. All people, organisations and messages here are fictional.

    Option 1: the online quiz (about 10 minutes).

    1. Open the Phishing Quiz made by Jigsaw, a Google unit: https://phishingquiz.withgoogle.com
    2. If it asks for a name or email address, use made-up details. Do not enter your real passwords or details anywhere in the quiz.
    3. Work through the examples. For each one, decide whether it is phishing or legitimate, and read any explanation.
    4. Write down two clues you missed or learned.

    Option 2: if the quiz will not load, or is blocked on your network. For each fictional message, decide Phishing or Legitimate, and write the clue that decided it.

    1. Email. Sender: security@bank-alerts.example. Subject: “Your account will be closed in 2 hours”. Body: “Dear customer, confirm your details now using the link below or lose access.” The link text says www.yourbank.example but the real destination shows login-check.example.
    2. Text. “Hi Sam, it’s your dentist’s office. Your appointment is tomorrow at 10:30 am. Reply C to confirm or call us on the number on your appointment card.” You do have an appointment booked for tomorrow.
    3. Email. Sender: ceo@your-company.example. Subject: “Quick favour”. Body: “I’m in a meeting and cannot talk. Please buy 5 gift cards for a client and send me the codes. Keep this between us.” You normally get emails from the CEO from a different address.
    4. Email. Sender: noreply@university.example. Subject: “Your library book is due on Friday”. Body addresses you by your full name and gives the book title, which you did borrow. There is no link. It says “Log in to your library account in the usual way to renew.”
    5. Voicemail transcript. “This is the tax office. A warrant has been issued for your arrest. Press 1 now or pay in gift cards to avoid legal action.”
    6. Email. Sender: help@streamingservice.example. Subject: “Your receipt”. Body: a receipt for a monthly subscription you have had for a year, with the same amount as usual. At the bottom: “If you did not make this payment, open the app and go to Settings. Do not reply to this email.”

    Option 1 (example clues, yours may differ): the sender’s address did not match the company it claimed to be from; a link’s real destination (seen by hovering over it) differed from its label; the message created urgency or fear; the greeting was generic instead of using your name; a legitimate email gave you a way to check without clicking anything.

    Option 2:

    # Verdict Clue
    1 Phishing Fear and a short deadline, a generic greeting, and the real link destination does not match the label.
    2 Legitimate It matches an appointment you really have, it does not ask for personal details, and it points you to a number you already trust.
    3 Phishing It borrows authority, adds urgency and secrecy, asks for gift cards, and comes from an address that differs from the usual one.
    4 Legitimate It matches a book you really borrowed, has no link, and tells you to log in the usual way.
    5 Phishing Real tax offices do not threaten arrest by voicemail or ask for payment in gift cards. This is fear and urgency.
    6 Legitimate It matches a subscription you really have and tells you to check through the app, not by replying.

    Legitimate messages usually let you check without clicking anything. If in doubt, contact the organisation yourself.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Name the tactic (10 minutes)

    All five scenarios are fictional. For each one, name the tactic (choose from phishing, pretexting, baiting, tailgating, quid pro quo) and give one reason in a sentence that points to a detail in the scenario.

    1. The helpful voice. Maya, an accounts clerk, gets a call from a man who says he is from “IT support”. He says her account has been hacked and he needs to fix it now. To do so, he asks her to read out the six-digit code that has just arrived on her phone.
    2. The full hands. Jo is about to swipe into the office when a man in a courier jacket, carrying three large boxes, says, “Sorry, my hands are full. Can you hold the door?” He walks in behind her.
    3. The lost drive. Ali finds a USB drive in the building lobby with a label that reads “Staff bonuses: confidential”. Curious, he plugs it into his work computer.
    4. The free upgrade. A caller tells Chen that his company is offering free security upgrades to staff this month. To start the upgrade, the caller asks Chen for his username and password.
    5. The parcel text. Rina gets a text: “We missed you! Your parcel is held. Pay a $2.95 redelivery fee within 24 hours: pay-parcel.example/xyz”. She has not ordered anything.

    For a stretch, name the lever (or levers) in each scenario too.

    # Tactic Reason
    1 Pretexting The caller invented a believable story (a hack and a fix) as cover to get a security code. It is also a phone call, so some people call it vishing.
    2 Tailgating He followed an authorised person through a secure door by asking for a polite favour.
    3 Baiting The USB drive was left as a tempting object, and the label played on curiosity.
    4 Quid pro quo The caller offered something in exchange (a free upgrade) for something the attacker wanted (login details).
    5 Phishing A fake message created urgency, and the link would lead to a fake payment page. By text, it is sometimes called smishing.

    Where two tactics fit, a well-reasoned alternative is acceptable. Scenario 1 could be called vishing (a scam phone call), and scenario 4 could be called pretexting because the caller invents a story. What matters is that your reason points to a detail in the scenario.

    Levers (one way to see them): 1 authority and fear; 2 helpfulness; 3 curiosity; 4 reward; 5 urgency and fear.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Trusting the logo or the look. Anyone can copy a logo. Check the sender, the link and what is being asked of you.
    • Judging only by spelling mistakes. Many fake messages have perfect spelling, and some real messages have errors.
    • Calling every scam “phishing”. Phishing is a fake message. A phone call with an invented story is pretexting. A follower at a door is tailgating.
    • Choosing a tactic with no reason. Always say which detail in the scenario shows the tactic.
    • Marking something “legitimate” because it names a real company. Attackers name real companies on purpose.
    • Forgetting the safe step. In real life the safe step is to contact the organisation yourself, using a phone number or app you already trust.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Lena works at the front desk of a clinic. A man in a high-visibility vest stands at the staff door with no pass. He says he is here to check the fire extinguishers and asks her to let him through because he is running late. What should Lena do?

      • A. Let him in, because a high-visibility vest shows he has a job to do.
      • B. Let him in, but ask him to be quick so he does not disturb patients.
      • C. Ask him to sign in at reception, and call the manager to confirm his visit.
      • D. Ask him to wait outside until the next staff member arrives to let him in himself.

    2. An employee receives an email: “Your mailbox is full. Click here within 1 hour or you will lose all your email.” Which two levers is the attacker using most?

      • A. Curiosity and reward, because the message promises something very interesting to open.
      • B. Helpfulness and authority, because it appears to come from a colleague.
      • C. Reward and curiosity, because the employee might gain more storage.
      • D. Urgency and fear, because of the deadline and the threat of losing email.

    3. A caller tells Dan, a receptionist, that she is from the building’s security company. She knows the name of Dan’s manager and the date of last month’s fire drill, then asks him to read out the door keypad code “to test the new system”. Which stage of the attack explains how she knew those details?

      • A. Research
      • B. The exploit
      • C. The exit
      • D. Tailgating
    1. C. A sign-in and a call to someone who would know the booking test his story without being rude, and they leave the decision with the clinic. A vest is easy to buy, so option A fails. Option B trusts his promise, which gives the attacker what they want. Option D delays him but does not check his story, and another staff member might let him in without checking either.
    2. D. A one-hour deadline is urgency, and “you will lose all your email” is fear. Nothing in the message is intriguing or offers a benefit (options A and C), and it does not claim to come from a colleague or boss (option B). If a message rushes you, slow down.
    3. A. She gathered small facts earlier and used them to build trust. The exploit is the keypad request itself, the exit comes afterwards, and tailgating is a different tactic, not a stage.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one or two prompts and write 3 to 6 sentences for each. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords.

    • Think of a time a message or call tried to rush you. Which lever was it using, and what did you do? What would you do now?
    • Why might someone who has been tricked hesitate to report it? What would make your workplace, club or family a place where people report quickly?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 25 minutes, including a pause after the lever table to ask for one real example from the room. Exercises 30 minutes: Spot the phish 10, Name the tactic 10, quick check 5, discussion 5.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners call every scam “phishing”. Use the common-mistakes box to separate the tactics.
    • Learners believe a message is real if the spelling is good or the logo is right. Show that both are cheap to fake.
    • Learners think reporting is an admission of failure. Say clearly that a fast report is a good outcome.
    • In the Name the tactic challenge, several scenarios fit two tactics. Accept a well-reasoned alternative.

    Option 1 of Spot the phish needs internet access. If the room’s network blocks it, use Option 2 as a group exercise and vote on each message.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. Ask pairs which lever they find hardest to resist, and write the answers where everyone can see them.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • National Cyber Security Centre (2024) Phishing attacks: defending your organisation explains layered defence. It is written for technical staff, so skim the technical detail.
    • National Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Phishing scams: how to spot and report them is a shorter page for the general public.
    • Australian Cyber Security Centre: cyber.gov.au.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 1 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • Social engineering attacks trust, habits and emotions instead of technology.
    • Attackers pull levers such as authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness, curiosity and reward, often in combination. Feeling rushed is a warning sign.
    • Name a tactic by what the attacker does: a fake message is phishing, an invented story is pretexting, a tempting object is baiting, following through a door is tailgating, and a trade of favours is quid pro quo.
    • Attacks follow four stages: research, building trust, the exploit and the exit.
    • Slow down, check by a different route, and report quickly. A fast report is a good outcome.

    References

    National Cyber Security Centre (2024) Phishing attacks: defending your organisation. Available at: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/phishing (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    National Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Phishing scams: how to spot and report them. Available at: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Identity, identity management and identity theft

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is an identity online, and how does identity theft happen?
    • How does an organisation decide who can open what?
    • How does one stolen identity harm individuals, groups and organisations?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • explain what an identity is online, using attributes, credentials and accounts (ULO 1)
    • describe how identity theft happens and trace its damage at the individual, group and organisational levels (ULO 1)
    • explain how identity and access management works at work, including authentication, authorisation, least privilege and the joiner, mover, leaver cycle (ULO 1)

    This episode matches Week 2 of The Human Firewall microcredential. The second half of the week is in the next episode, The insider threat. It builds on the three levels (individual, group, organisation) from Digital lives and the tricks from Social engineering.

    Who are you, online?

    Your identity online is not one thing. It is a bundle of three parts.

    Part What it is Examples Can you change it?
    Attributes Information about you. Who you are. Name, date of birth, address, student number Hard or impossible. You cannot get a new date of birth.
    Credentials What you use to prove you are you. How you prove it. Password, fingerprint, a code sent to your phone Yes, if you notice in time. A password can change in minutes.
    Accounts Where you use your identity. Where it lives. Email, bank login, a game profile Each is a separate identity that the organisation behind it recognises.

    This matters because attributes cannot be replaced, so once they leak they stay leaked. Credentials can be replaced, and the more accounts you hold, the more places someone can try to pretend to be you.

    Identity theft

    Identity theft means using another person’s personal details to pretend to be them, usually to get money, goods or services. A criminal might open a phone plan in your name, apply for credit, or take over your email so they can reset all your other passwords.

    Where do the details come from? Sometimes from a data breach at a company you trusted. Sometimes from a phishing message or a phone call, like the ones in the last episode. Sometimes from something much simpler, such as a photo of an ID card sent by email or papers thrown out without shredding. Criminals often join up small pieces: a name from one leak, a birthday from another, an address from a social media post.

    Use the three levels to follow the damage.

    • Individual. Money, time and stress, and a credit record that can take months to fix. Victims often have to prove to several organisations that they did not open the accounts. Many feel embarrassed even though it was not their fault.
    • Group. A stolen identity is a weapon. A criminal inside your email can message everyone you know, and they will trust it because it looks like you.
    • Organisation. The bank or phone company that was fooled has losses, investigation time and a loss of customer trust.

    Notice how the levels link. One person’s stolen identity becomes a loss for a company and a worry for everyone in the contact list. The first challenge asks you to trace exactly this kind of chain.

    Identity and access management at work

    How does an organisation keep track of who is who, and who can open what? It uses identity and access management, or IAM. In plain terms, IAM is the set of rules, processes and tools that make sure the right people have the right access, to the right things, at the right time, and nobody else does (Wang, [2008]).

    IAM has two halves.

    • Identity management is about the identities themselves: creating an account when someone starts, updating it when their job changes, and closing it when they leave.
    • Access management is about what each identity can do. It has two steps. Authentication asks: are you really who you say you are? Authorisation asks: now that we know who you are, what are you allowed to open?

    Three ways to prove who you are

    • Something you know, such as a password.
    • Something you have, such as a phone or a security key.
    • Something you are, such as a fingerprint.

    Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means using two or more different kinds. A password plus a code from your phone is two kinds. A password plus a PIN is not, because both are things you know. (Wang’s slides count any combination as strong. This lesson uses the stricter rule, which is the one security teams use in practice.)

    Single sign-on gives you one login for several services. It is convenient, but if that login is stolen the attacker reaches them all, so it needs strong protection such as MFA.

    Least privilege

    A key idea in authorisation is least privilege: give each person only the access they need to do their job, and no more. It sounds strict, but it limits the damage if that person makes a mistake, is tricked, or turns bad.

    Joiner, mover, leaver

    IAM follows people through their working life.

    • Joiner. A new person gets the access their role needs.
    • Mover. When someone changes jobs inside the organisation, their access should change too.
    • Leaver. When someone leaves, every account should be closed straight away.

    Each step is a place where things go wrong: new starters given far too much, movers who collect old access like souvenirs, and leavers whose accounts stay open for months. Each person should also have their own account. If three people share one login and something goes wrong, nobody can tell who did it.

    There is a privacy side too. An employer that manages your identity can also record when you log in and what you open. That is often reasonable, but how much should it see? The discussion at the end asks you to think about it.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Map the damage in an identity-theft case (15 minutes)

    Content note. This case is about identity theft and its effect on a person. If that topic is upsetting, for example because it has happened to you or someone close to you, use the alternative case at the end of this challenge instead. Everyone and every organisation named here is fictional.

    The case: Dana and the fake phone plan. Dana Pereira, 24, shares a rented house with two flatmates. Last spring she sent a photo of her driver licence to a flatshare website, NestFinder, to prove her identity when she applied for a room. NestFinder later told its users that an employee’s laptop had been stolen and that some uploaded documents may have been exposed.

    Three months afterwards, a criminal combined Dana’s licence details with her date of birth and address from an old social media post. Pretending to be Dana, the criminal opened a mobile phone plan with a company called Bluegum Mobile and took two expensive phones on a 24-month contract. The phones were posted to an empty rental property.

    Next, the criminal used the “forgot password” link on Dana’s email account. The code was sent to her old mobile number, which the criminal had also taken over. From her email, the criminal messaged her flatmates and her work team, saying she was stuck overseas and needed money urgently. One flatmate sent $400 before checking with Dana in person.

    Dana found out when a debt collector rang about the unpaid phone bills. She spent several weeks proving to Bluegum Mobile, her bank and a credit reporting body that she had not opened the plan. During that time she was refused a small loan for a car repair. Bluegum Mobile wrote off the cost of the phones, and its fraud team spent days on the case.

    1. Read the case (3 minutes).
    2. Fill in a table (7 minutes) with at least three rows and three columns: “Who was affected”, “What damage?” and “Which detail in the case shows this?”. Name at least two different effects at the individual level, and at least one effect for the group and for each organisation you list.
    3. Find one effect that lasts (1 minute): one that could continue for months or years.
    4. Write 3 to 4 sentences (4 minutes) answering: Follow the chain. How did something that happened to Dana become a problem for another level?

    Alternative case. Palette Post is a fictional online art-supplies shop. A fault in its website exposed its customer list, with names, addresses and dates of birth, for several weeks. Criminals used some of the details to open accounts with a fictional buy-now-pay-later company, PayLater Co, and buy goods that were never paid for. PayLater Co wrote off the losses. Palette Post emailed all customers, set up a help line and paid for a security review, and many customers wrote that they would shop elsewhere. A hobby painting club that ordered through the shop found its members receiving scam emails that named the club. Do steps 2 to 4 with this case.

    One worked answer. You may group the effects differently, as long as each one points to a detail in the case.

    Level Who was affected What damage? Detail in the case
    Individual Dana Money and credit: chased for phone debts she did not owe, and refused a small loan The debt collector’s call; the refused car-repair loan
    Individual Dana Time and stress: weeks of proving she was not the customer, to three organisations “Several weeks proving to Bluegum Mobile, her bank and a credit reporting body”
    Individual Dana Loss of control of her accounts: her email and mobile number were taken over The “forgot password” code went to the number the criminal controlled
    Group Dana’s flatmates and work team Money and trust: one flatmate lost $400, and people may now doubt messages from Dana or from each other The “stuck overseas” message sent from her real email
    Organisation Bluegum Mobile Financial loss and staff time: it wrote off two phones, and its fraud team spent days on it “Wrote off the cost of the phones”; “its fraud team spent days”
    Organisation NestFinder Reputation and customer trust (possible): it had to tell users that documents may have been exposed. The case does not say whether it lost customers The laptop theft and its announcement to users

    The effect that lasts. A debt or fraud flag on Dana’s credit record could stay until it is disputed and corrected. She was already refused a loan during the dispute, so this effect had started. Lower trust in online services, or her flatmates’ caution about money requests, may also last. The case does not say these happened, so say “may” if you use them.

    Short answer (example). Dana’s licence photo, which she gave NestFinder to get a room, may have been exposed, and her licence details were later used to impersonate her. So what happened to her became a loss for Bluegum Mobile, which was fooled into handing over phones. Taking over her email turned Dana into a weapon against her own contacts, because her flatmates trusted a message that looked like it came from her. That group effect cost one flatmate $400 and damaged the group’s trust. The chain may be: details possibly exposed through NestFinder, then an individual’s identity stolen, then a group’s money and trust, then another organisation’s losses.

    NestFinder could also be placed as the source of the problem instead of a victim. Either choice is fine if your reason points to a detail in the case.

    Alternative case. Individual: a customer may face unpaid-debt letters (money), time spent correcting records, and worry. A lasting effect is that the leaked date of birth cannot be changed. Group: the painting club’s members receive scam emails naming the club, so they may trust club messages less. Organisation: PayLater Co lost money on the written-off goods, and Palette Post paid for a help line and a review and faced customers saying they would leave. The chain: the website fault exposed customers’ details, which led to accounts being opened in their names, and customers’ decision to leave then affects the shop.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Listing one effect only. “Dana lost money” is one effect. Add time, stress or lost control of her accounts.
    • Putting the flatmates under “individual”. They are affected through their link to Dana, so they are the group. Name them and say what happened to them.
    • Listing costs with no link to the case. “The company may be fined” does not use a detail from the story. Tie each effect to something in it.
    • Saying “everyone was affected”. Name each person or organisation and say how they were affected.
    • Missing the chain. Say how the harm at one level caused harm at the next.
    • Treating “lasting” as “big”. A lasting effect is one that continues, such as a damaged credit record, not just one that was large.
    Challenge

    Challenge: Joiner, mover, leaver (10 minutes)

    A fictional scenario. Kai starts as a receptionist at a small accounting firm. Eighteen months later, Kai moves to the payroll team. Two years after that, Kai resigns and leaves on a Friday.

    1. For each of the three steps, write what access Kai should have, or what should happen to it (3 minutes).
    2. Now suppose the firm did nothing at the mover and leaver steps. Name one thing that could go wrong at each step (4 minutes).
    3. Choose one habit or control that would stop each problem (3 minutes).

    One worked answer.

    Step What should happen What could go wrong if skipped A control that helps
    Joiner Kai gets only what a receptionist needs, such as the diary, the shared inbox and the visitor log. Giving Kai “the same access as the last receptionist” brings years of extra access along. Least privilege: give access by role, and add more only when asked and approved.
    Mover Kai’s reception access is removed, and payroll access is added. Kai keeps the old access and now holds both sets. Access builds up like souvenirs, so one stolen login opens far more than it should. A review of access whenever someone changes role, with the manager signing off the new list.
    Leaver Every account is closed on Kai’s last day, and shared passwords Kai knew are changed. An open account can be misused by Kai, or by a criminal who finds old credentials. Nobody notices because nobody is watching it. A leaver checklist that includes closing accounts on the same day, owned by a named person.

    The key habit is that access follows the job, not the person. Each step needs someone who owns it, or nobody does it.

    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. A company wants multi-factor authentication for its remote staff. Which pair of checks uses two different kinds of proof?

      • A. A password and a security question about the first school attended.
      • B. A passphrase and a four-digit PIN that the user chooses.
      • C. A password and a second password that must change every month.
      • D. A password and a code from an app on the staff member’s phone.

    2. Rosa learns that her details have leaked from an old online account. Which of these could she replace most easily if it were misused?

      • A. Her date of birth.
      • B. Her password.
      • C. Her birthplace.
      • D. Her full name.

    3. Lucia logs in to her work account with her password and a code from her phone. She then tries to open the finance folder and sees “access denied”. Which part of access management said no?

      • A. Authentication.
      • B. Multi-factor authentication.
      • C. Authorisation.
      • D. Identity management.
    1. D. A password is something you know, and the code from the phone is something you have. Two different kinds mean a stolen password alone is not enough. Options A, B and C all pair two things you know, which is one kind of proof used twice. A security question can also be found out from social media.
    2. B. A password is a credential, so Rosa can change it in minutes. Her date of birth, birthplace and name are attributes, and they stay the same for life.
    3. C. The system knew exactly who Lucia was, because she had passed authentication. It simply had not given her permission for that folder, which is authorisation. Option B describes how she proved who she was, and option D is about creating and closing accounts.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one prompt and write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not share private details such as passwords, card numbers or account details.

    • Your employer and your identity. Many employers manage the account you use at work, and can see when you log in and what you open. How much privacy do you think you give up when your employer manages your identity? What would you want to be told? What limits would seem fair?
    • Identity or card theft. Has someone you know ever had an identity or card stolen, or come close? You do not have to share any details. Think privately about what would be the hardest part if it happened to you. You may write only what you are comfortable with, or simply move on.

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: Dana case 15, joiner-mover-leaver 10, quick check 5, discussion 5 (2 minutes of quiet writing and 3 minutes of sharing).

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners mix up authentication and authorisation. Use Lucia: the system knew who she was and still said no.
    • Learners think a “password plus PIN” is multi-factor. Ask them to name the kind of proof for each.
    • Learners list effects with no link to the case. Ask “which sentence in the case tells you that?”
    • Learners put the flatmates under “individual”. Ask what connects them to Dana.

    Sensitive topic. Identity theft is personal and some learners will have experienced it. Say before the case that the alternative case is always available and nobody needs to explain why they chose it. Do not ask learners to share their own experiences in the second discussion prompt. Offer IDCARE (see Go deeper) to anyone who needs support.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. On the employer prompt, ask the room to agree what an employer should tell staff about logging, and what limits are fair. There is no single right answer.

    If you are short of time. Drop the joiner-mover-leaver challenge and keep the Dana case.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Wang, K. ([2008]) Identity and Access Management is a short slide deck for technical managers. Read the slides on identity management and access management, and skip the vendor and market slides. The file is at http://www.cpd.iit.edu/netsecure08/KEVIN_WANG.pdf. That site opens only over http, so it is not a clickable link here and your browser may warn that the page is “Not secure”.
    • Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Identity theft explains how it happens and what to do.
    • IDCARE is Australia and New Zealand’s national identity and cyber support service. It is free to use, and a good place to start if this has happened to you.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 2 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • An online identity has three parts: attributes (who you are), credentials (how you prove it) and accounts (where you use it). Attributes cannot be replaced, and credentials can.
    • Identity theft means using someone’s details to pretend to be them. The harm spreads from the individual to their group and to the organisations that were fooled.
    • Authentication checks who you are, and authorisation decides what you may open. Multi-factor means two or more different kinds of proof.
    • Least privilege means each person gets the access their job needs and no more.
    • Access should follow the job through joiner, mover and leaver steps, and each step needs an owner.

    References

    Wang, K. ([2008]) Identity and Access Management. Available at: http://www.cpd.iit.edu/netsecure08/KEVIN_WANG.pdf (Accessed: 2 November 2026). The year is inferred from the conference name in the web address.

    Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Identity theft. Available at: https://www.cyber.gov.au/threats/types-threats/identity-theft (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    IDCARE (n.d.) IDCARE: national identity and cyber support service. Available at: https://www.idcare.org/ (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from The insider threat

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Who is an insider, and why are insiders such a difficult problem?
    • How do malicious, negligent and compromised insiders differ, and what control suits each?
    • What is espionage, and why do organisations take it seriously?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • tell malicious, negligent and compromised insiders apart (ULO 1)
    • choose a sensible control for each type of insider, and explain why it fits (ULO 1)
    • explain the difference between corporate and state espionage, and why organisations take both seriously (ULO 1)

    This episode matches Week 2 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Identity, identity management and identity theft, and it uses ideas from that episode: least privilege, multi-factor authentication and the joiner, mover, leaver cycle.

    Who is an insider?

    An insider is anyone who has legitimate access to an organisation’s systems, buildings or information. That includes employees, but also contractors, suppliers’ staff, volunteers, and former staff whose access was never removed.

    Why are insiders such a problem? Insiders already have access, they know the organisation and where its valuable information is kept, and what they do tends to look like normal work. Colwill (2009), in a paper that appears to take the viewpoint of a large company’s security team, also points out that loyalty can change when an organisation, or the economy around it, goes through change, so even long-serving people may come under pressure. The paper argues that technical controls on their own are not enough.

    Three types of insider

    Security people usually describe three types. Learn these, because you will use them in the challenges.

    Type What happened Typical examples
    Malicious The person causes harm on purpose. Motives include money, revenge for something that went wrong at work, or loyalty to someone outside. Copying a client list before joining a competitor. Deleting files after a dispute.
    Negligent The person causes harm by accident, usually without meaning any harm at all. Emailing a file to the wrong person. Taking a shortcut to meet a deadline. Leaving a laptop on a train.
    Compromised The person is a victim. An outsider has taken over their account or device and is using the access while the person has no idea. A login stolen through phishing or a reused password. Software installed by a bad attachment.

    The negligent type is often the most common, and it is a human-factors problem, not a villain problem. When people take risky shortcuts, ask why. Often the safe way is slow or awkward.

    The compromised type is a reminder that the login belongs to the insider but the hands on the keyboard do not. Treat the account takeover as the main problem, not the person.

    The question that sorts the types is simple: did the person mean to cause harm, and did they know it was happening?

    Can insiders be controlled?

    Can you ever stop insider attacks completely? Probably not, because you cannot run an organisation without trusting anyone. But you can reduce, detect and respond. Each of these is a control, which means something an organisation does to lower a risk.

    • Least privilege, so each person can only reach what they need.
    • Closing accounts quickly when people leave.
    • Multi-factor authentication, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
    • Two-person approval for high-risk actions such as large payments. Think of a shop where one person takes the money and a second checks the count. Neither can easily cheat alone.
    • Logging and checking. Keep logs, and look at them.
    • Making the safe way the easy way, so staff do not need shortcuts.

    Review everyone’s access from time to time, because trust can change. Culture matters as much as tools. People who feel treated fairly are less likely to turn against their employer, and people who are not afraid of blame report mistakes sooner.

    Espionage

    Espionage means secretly getting information that someone wants to keep private.

    • Corporate espionage is carried out for a business, to get a competitor’s designs, prices, client lists or plans.
    • State espionage is carried out for a government, to get political, military or economic secrets.

    The two sometimes overlap, for example when a government wants a country’s industry to gain an edge. Small firms are targets too. They may hold valuable designs, or supply larger organisations, so breaking into a supplier can be a way into its bigger customer.

    How real is the threat? Governments and security agencies treat it as real, because information is valuable and people are often the easiest way to reach it. Spies may use technical attacks, but they also use human tactics: a friendly stranger at a conference, a fake recruiter, a gift, a favour, or pressure on someone with money worries. These are the social-engineering tactics from episode 2, aimed at a patient target.

    Espionage usually involves breaking the law, for example by stealing confidential information, bribing someone or hacking into systems. It is not just tough competition. If someone offers you money for your employer’s secrets, the right move is to say no and tell your manager or security team.

    Challenge

    Challenge, part A: Classify the insider (10 minutes)

    All six profiles are fictional. For each one, write the type (malicious, negligent or compromised) and one reason that points to a detail in the profile. Ask yourself: did the person mean to cause harm? Did they know it was happening?

    1. Leon, sales manager. Leon has accepted a job at a competitor and starts there in a month. Over two weekends he copies the full client list and price sheets from the company system to his personal cloud storage. He plans to contact the clients once he has moved.
    2. Hana, project officer. The remote-access system at Hana’s company is slow, and she has a deadline. She emails a spreadsheet of customers’ names and phone numbers to her personal email address so that she can work on it at home. She tells no one.
    3. Wes, warehouse supervisor. Wes reused one password on his work login and on a hobby forum. The forum was hacked and its passwords were leaked. At 3 am, someone logs in as Wes from another country and starts browsing the stock and supplier files. Wes is asleep.
    4. Ruth, former contract administrator. Ruth’s contract ended after a dispute over pay. Nobody closed her account. Two weeks later, she logs in from home and deletes a shared project folder, saying afterwards that “they deserved it”.
    5. Mei, junior developer. Mei is stuck on a coding problem. She pastes a block of the company’s code, including a secret access key, into a public question-and-answer website, hoping a stranger will help. She had not noticed the key was in it.
    6. Alicia, executive assistant. Alicia opens an invoice attachment that looks like it came from a regular supplier. It quietly installs software that copies her emails to an outside address. She notices nothing unusual.

    One worked answer. The type is the key answer. The reason should point to a detail in the profile.

    # Type Reason
    1 Malicious Leon is acting on purpose, to take clients to a competitor.
    2 Negligent Hana did not intend harm. She took a shortcut because the safe route was too slow, and broke the rules.
    3 Compromised A criminal is using Wes’s login while he sleeps. The leak and the reused password gave them access, and Wes did not act.
    4 Malicious Ruth meant to cause harm. Her motive was anger over the dispute.
    5 Negligent Mei did not mean to leak the key. She did not notice it was in the code.
    6 Compromised An outsider’s software is using Alicia’s access. She is a victim and has no idea.

    Where two types might seem to fit. Only profile 3 has a genuine alternative. The best answer is compromised, because a criminal is using Wes’s login. If you said negligent because he reused a password, that can be accepted when your reason mentions the reused password and your control fits, for example a password manager and training on not reusing passwords. Profile 5 has no alternative. The profile says Mei had not noticed the key, so she did not intend the leak, and calling her malicious does not fit the facts.

    Challenge

    Challenge, part B: Choose the control (10 minutes)

    For each of the six profiles in part A, choose one control that fits the type and the case. Write one sentence on why it would help. Think about the controls in the teaching text: least privilege, closing accounts promptly, multi-factor authentication, two-person approval, logging and checking, and making the safe way the easy way.

    One worked answer. Controls are a matter of judgement, so more than one answer can be right. Check that yours fits the type you chose and that you can say why it helps.

    # Type A control that fits
    1 Malicious Limit who can export the client list, and log and alert on large copies to personal storage. This is least privilege plus logging, checked more closely when someone resigns. A good alternative is reduced access once someone has resigned.
    2 Negligent Fix the slow remote access so the safe way is the easy way, and block attachments with customer data going to personal email addresses.
    3 Compromised Multi-factor authentication, so a leaked password alone is not enough. Alerts on logins from unusual places also help, and so does training on not reusing passwords.
    4 Malicious Close accounts on the day a contract ends. This is the “leaver” step of identity management.
    5 Negligent Automatic scanning that blocks secret keys in code before it can be posted, plus a clear safe place to ask for help, such as an internal forum.
    6 Compromised Filtering and scanning of email attachments, plus protection software on her computer. A “report it, no blame” culture also helps catch these cases quickly.

    A control that does not fit the case does not count. “Send staff on a training course” for profile 4 would not work, because Ruth knew exactly what she was doing.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Calling everything malicious. Most insider incidents are accidents, not attacks. Ask whether the person meant to cause harm.
    • Blaming the victim. A compromised insider is a victim. Treat the account takeover as the main problem, not the person.
    • Choosing “train staff” every time. Training helps negligent insiders but does little against someone who is acting on purpose or a criminal using a stolen login.
    • Choosing a control that does not match the case. “Two-person approval” does not stop a leaver logging in at home. Match the control to what went wrong.
    • Giving a reason with no detail. Point to a detail in the profile, such as “She did not notice the key”.
    • Forgetting the safe way. When staff take shortcuts, find out why. The best control often makes the safe way easier.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. A delivery planner prints a list of customers’ addresses and leaves it on a train by mistake. Nobody has misused it so far. Which type of insider is she?

      • A. Negligent, because she was careless with the list but meant no harm.
      • B. Malicious, because strangers now have the customers’ addresses.
      • C. Compromised, because the list is now outside the company’s control.
      • D. Malicious, because printing customer data breaks the company’s policy.

    2. A procurement officer sets up a fake supplier, then approves its invoices himself and pays them into a bank account he controls. Which control would most directly have prevented this?

      • A. A longer course on spotting phishing emails for all procurement staff.
      • B. A rule that a second person must approve new suppliers and payments.
      • C. A stricter password rule that makes staff change their passwords weekly.
      • D. A policy that bans staff from using personal phones at their desks.

    3. At a trade conference, a friendly stranger asks Tomas, an engineer, detailed questions about his firm’s unreleased product and offers to pay him for a copy of the plans. What should Tomas do?

      • A. Say no and tell his manager or security team.
      • B. Accept, because it is only competition between businesses.
      • C. Share only the parts that are not marked confidential.
      • D. Say nothing, because telling his employer might get him in trouble.
    1. A. She did not intend harm and nobody tricked her. Her carelessness put the list at risk, which is the mark of a negligent insider. Breaking a rule (option D) or the result of the mistake (option B) does not make someone malicious, and option C describes someone whose account has been taken over, which did not happen here.
    2. B. Two-person approval means one person alone cannot create and pay a fake supplier. It is a standard control against a malicious insider. Nobody tricked the officer, so phishing training (A) would not stop him. He used his own proper login, so a password rule (C) would not either. The fraud did not depend on personal phones (D).
    3. A. Offering money for an employer’s secrets is likely to be espionage, and espionage usually involves breaking the law. The right move is to say no and report it. Option B treats a crime as tough competition, option C still hands over information, and option D keeps a secret that the security team needs to know about.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one or two prompts and write 3 to 6 sentences for each. Do not name other people or share private details.

    • Insiders. Who do you think carries out insider attacks, and why? Can they ever be controlled completely, or only reduced? Which type do you think organisations most underestimate?
    • Espionage. Why does corporate or state espionage happen, and how real do you think the threat is? Where does criminal behaviour fit in? Does it change how you think about your own work, or about being approached by a stranger who asks about your job?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 25 minutes. Exercises 30 minutes: classify 10, choose the control 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Learners can do part A and part B on the same sheet.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners call everything malicious. Keep asking “did the person mean to cause harm?”
    • Learners call Wes negligent because he reused a password. Accept this only if the reason names the reuse and the control fits. The best answer is compromised, because a criminal is the one acting.
    • Learners choose “train staff” for every case. Ask what training would have done for Ruth.
    • Learners blame compromised insiders. Remind them that the person is a victim, and that blame stops people from reporting.
    • Learners think espionage only happens to governments. Mention the small supplier example.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. Do not make the discussion about real organisations or named people. If someone shares a workplace story, ask them to leave out names. The question “which type do organisations most underestimate?” often produces a useful split between negligent and compromised.

    Link to the previous episode. The joiner, mover, leaver cycle (episode 3) is the answer to profile 4. Point this out when learners choose controls.

    If you are short of time. Run part A as a whole-room activity, calling out each profile for a show of hands, and keep part B for pairs.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (n.d.) Defining insider threats is a plain-language US government explanation, with the same types of insider in different words.
    • ASIO is Australia’s security intelligence agency. Its website explains the espionage and foreign interference threat to Australians.
    • Australian Government (n.d.) Protective Security Policy Framework shows how government manages the risk of trusted insiders. We return to it in a later episode.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 2 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • An insider is anyone with legitimate access, including contractors, volunteers and former staff whose access was never closed.
    • There are three types: malicious (on purpose), negligent (by accident) and compromised (a victim whose access is used by an outsider).
    • To sort a case, ask whether the person meant to cause harm and knew it was happening.
    • You cannot remove the insider threat, but you can reduce, detect and respond, with controls that fit the type: least privilege, prompt account closing, multi-factor authentication, two-person approval, logging, and making the safe way easy.
    • Espionage is spying for a business or a government. It usually involves crime, and it uses the same human tactics as social engineering. If you are approached, say no and tell your manager or security team.

    References

    Colwill, C. (2009) ‘Human factors in information security: the insider threat – who can you trust these days?’, Information Security Technical Report, 14(4), pp. 186–196. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.istr.2010.04.004.

    Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (n.d.) Defining insider threats. Available at: https://www.cisa.gov/topics/physical-security/insider-threat-mitigation/defining-insider-threats (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    ASIO (n.d.) Australian Security Intelligence Organisation. Available at: https://www.asio.gov.au/ (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Australian Government (n.d.) Protective Security Policy Framework. Available at: https://www.protectivesecurity.gov.au/ (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Attack techniques and human defences

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do attackers get in through direct access, identity theft, phishing and social engineering?
    • Which human defence best answers each technique?
    • Why do espionage and insider approaches depend on people as much as on technology?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • describe common direct-access attacks, identity theft, phishing and social engineering (ULO 1)
    • match each attack technique to the human defence that fits it best, and name a sensible backup (ULO 1)
    • explain why layers of defence, including people, work better than any single defence (ULO 1)

    This episode matches Week 3 of The Human Firewall microcredential. The second half of the week is in the next episode, Privacy and privacy impact assessments. It builds on the tricks from Social engineering and the ideas in Identity, identity management and identity theft.

    Direct access: the oldest attack

    So far you have seen how attackers trick people, and how identity theft and insiders do damage. This episode pulls those ideas together. How do attackers actually get in? And what can ordinary people do to stop them?

    Start with the oldest attack of all. Direct access means the attacker reaches a device, a room or a piece of paper in person. No clever hacking is needed. There are five techniques to know.

    Technique What it is Why it works
    Tailgating Following an authorised person through a secure door People are polite and hold the door.
    Shoulder surfing Watching someone type a password or PIN, or reading their screen Screens and keypads are often in public view.
    Walk-up access Using a computer or phone that someone left unlocked or unattended It takes a few seconds and needs no skill.
    Baiting Leaving a tempting item, such as a USB stick labelled “Salaries”, where someone will find it and plug it in Curiosity is hard to resist.
    Bin raiding Searching rubbish or recycling for papers with names, account numbers or passwords Many people throw papers away without a second thought.

    The best defences here are habits, and none of them needs special equipment.

    • Challenge people you do not recognise, politely, and ask them to sign in or wait for a staff member.
    • Lock your screen every time you stand up, and shield your screen and keypad from view.
    • Never plug in a device you found. Hand it to your IT team.
    • Shred papers that carry personal details.

    These habits only work if people remember them, and if people feel allowed to say, “Sorry, who are you here to see?”

    Messages and calls

    Some attacks arrive through a message or a call instead. You met identity theft in Identity, identity management and identity theft. It is an outcome: a criminal uses your personal details to pretend to be you. The ways in include a data breach, a phishing message, a call from someone pretending to be your bank, or papers from the bin. Criminals also try a password you used on one site on every other site, which is why one leak can open many accounts.

    Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into clicking, logging in or paying. Social engineering is the wider idea: tricking a person rather than a machine. It includes pretexting, where the attacker invents a believable story, such as “I’m from IT support”.

    These tactics lean on urgency, authority and trust. Picture a caller who says, “I’m from the bank’s fraud team, and I need to confirm your card number to stop a payment.” The story is urgent and official, but a real bank would not ask for that on a call you did not start. Another version is a caller who says she is from head office and is doing an urgent audit, and she needs the staff phone list straight away. Again the hook is authority and urgency.

    The human defence has three steps.

    1. Pause. Attackers want you to rush.
    2. Verify. Use a phone number or website you already trust, never the one in the message.
    3. Report. People who report a mistake within minutes can save an organisation days of damage, but only if they are not afraid of blame. That is why good organisations say “report it, no blame”.

    Two more defences matter for identity theft. Use a different password for every account, with a password manager if you can, and turn on multi-factor authentication. And share less. Every detail you post or keep is a detail that can be joined to another, so a pet’s name, a birthday and a suburb may each look harmless alone.

    Layers: people and technology together

    No single defence is enough. Security people talk about layers. Technology, such as email filters and locked doors, catches many attacks. People catch the rest, and they are often the last layer. If one layer fails, another should catch the problem.

    A locked door does nothing if someone holds it open. A strong password does nothing if you read it out to a caller. That is why this course spends so much time on human defences.

    Espionage and the human element

    Button (2020) is an editorial about economic and industrial espionage. It is behind a paywall, so this episode only summarises it in our own words.

    Economic espionage means stealing secrets to benefit a foreign state. Industrial espionage means stealing them to benefit a private business, such as a competitor. The two overlap. Button describes methods that range from legal ones to illegal ones, such as hacking and approaching insiders with bribes. He also notes that victims often under-report, and may not realise they were targeted, which makes espionage hard to measure. By comparison, studying a rival’s public information, such as its annual report, is generally legal.

    Notice how much of this is about people. A bribed insider or a successful phishing email is a human weakness being used. The defences are the ones you already know: limit access to what people need, watch for approaches, and make reporting safe. This is not only a problem for governments and large companies. A small firm may hold designs or client lists that are valuable, or may supply a bigger organisation, so it can be a way in.

    The editorial does not teach everyday defences such as challenging a visitor or reporting a phishing message. Those come from the rest of this episode and from the challenges below.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Match attacks to defences (15 minutes)

    Most attacks have a matching human defence: a habit that stops the attack or limits the damage. This challenge asks you to match them. All people in it are fictional.

    Content note: it mentions identity theft and scam calls in general terms. No victim is described. If the topic is upsetting, treat it as a pure matching exercise and skip the explanations.

    Attack techniques (rows)

    # Technique In one line
    1 Tailgating Following an authorised person through a secure door
    2 Shoulder surfing Watching someone type a password or reading their screen
    3 Walk-up access Using a computer or phone that was left unlocked or unattended
    4 Baiting Leaving a tempting item, such as a USB stick, for someone to plug in
    5 Bin raiding Searching rubbish or recycling for papers with personal details
    6 Phishing A fake email or text that tricks you into clicking, logging in or paying
    7 Pretexting by phone A caller invents a believable story, such as “I’m from IT support”, to get information
    8 Account takeover with a reused password A criminal tries a leaked password on your other accounts (a way of committing identity theft)

    Human defences (columns)

    Letter Defence
    A Challenge visitors politely and ask them to sign in. Do not hold doors for people you do not know
    B Lock your screen, shield it from view and keep your devices with you
    C Never plug in a device you found. Hand it to IT
    D Shred or securely dispose of papers with personal details
    E Use a different password for every account, plus multi-factor authentication
    F Pause, then verify through a phone number or website you already trust
    G Report straight away, with no blame
    H Share and keep less personal information

    1. Read the two tables (2 minutes).

    2. Fill in the matrix (13 minutes). Copy the grid below. For each technique, write 1st in the one column that is the best primary defence. Write 2nd in one other column that is a good backup (a second layer).

      Technique A B C D E F G H
      1 Tailgating
      2 Shoulder surfing
      3 Walk-up access
      4 Baiting
      5 Bin raiding
      6 Phishing
      7 Pretexting by phone
      8 Account takeover

    One worked answer. The primary defence is the key choice. The backup is a matter of judgement, so count yours as a match if it fits the technique and you can say why it helps.

    Technique Primary (1st) Backup (2nd) Why
    1 Tailgating A G The attack needs a person to hold the door, so challenging visitors stops it. Reporting a stranger who got in is a good second layer.
    2 Shoulder surfing B E Shielding the screen stops the watcher seeing the password. A different password plus a second check means a glimpsed password is not enough.
