    3 Walk-up access B G Locking the screen and keeping the device with you stops it. Reporting a lost device quickly limits the damage.
    4 Baiting C G The attack only works if someone plugs the item in. Telling IT about a found device helps them check for more.
    5 Bin raiding D H Shredding leaves nothing to find. Keeping fewer papers with personal details means less is there to find.
    6 Phishing F G Pausing and checking through a trusted channel beats the pressure to act fast. Reporting early protects colleagues too.
    7 Pretexting by phone F G or H Hang up and call back on a number you already trust. Reporting the call warns others. Sharing less also gives the caller less to use.
    8 Account takeover E G A different password for each account means one leak opens only one door. Reporting and checking accounts early limits the damage.

    Where two answers genuinely fit, both are acceptable. For phishing, E (multi-factor authentication) is also a good backup, because it limits the damage if a password is typed into a fake page. For bin raiding, H and G are both reasonable backups. For account takeover, H is also acceptable. A backup that does not fit the technique, such as C for phishing, does not match.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Mateo’s mornings (10 minutes)

    Mateo works at a small accounting firm. He usually holds the office door open for anyone carrying boxes, because “it would be rude not to”. When he goes to make a coffee, he leaves his laptop unlocked on his desk. And he uses the same password for his work login and for a hobby forum.

    1. Name the technique that each habit makes easier. Use the list in the previous challenge.
    2. Name the defence letter that would fix each habit.
    3. In one or two sentences, say which of the three changes you would ask Mateo to make first, and why.
    Habit 1. Technique it makes easier 2. Defence
    Holds the door for anyone Tailgating A
    Leaves his laptop unlocked at his desk Walk-up access B
    Uses the same password for work and a hobby forum Account takeover with a reused password E

    3. Example answer. All three are good answers if you give a reason. For example: “Start with E. A leaked forum password may already be out there, so the work account is at risk today, and a password manager makes it easy.” Or: “Start with B. Locking the screen takes two seconds and he can do it every time he stands up.” Any choice is sound if the reason points to a detail about Mateo.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Picking “report it” for everything. Reporting is a good backup, but it is rarely the best primary defence. Ask what stops the attack happening in the first place.
    • Matching a technology fix. This activity is about human defences, which are habits. Email filters and door locks help, but they are not in the matrix.
    • Mixing up the outcome and the technique. Identity theft is what a criminal achieves. In row 8 the technique is taking over an account with a reused password.
    • Putting 1st in more than one column. Choose the one defence that most directly stops the technique. Use 2nd for the second layer.
    • Treating tailgating as rude to challenge. A polite challenge, such as “Can I help you find someone?”, is the correct defence.
    • Skipping the reason. When you say which change comes first, point to a detail about Mateo rather than saying “it is the most important”.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Ines is in a café, typing a password into her laptop. A stranger at the next table reads her screen over her shoulder. Which technique is that?

      • A. Tailgating
      • B. Shoulder surfing
      • C. Baiting
      • D. Pretexting

    2. A flash drive in a gift box arrives by post at Pia’s workplace, addressed to her. A note says, “Your loyalty reward is on this drive.” She does not recognise the sender. What should she do?

      • A. Plug it into a spare computer first, to see what is on it.
      • B. Give it to IT without plugging it in, and say how it came.
      • C. Plug it in once, then delete the files if they look odd.
      • D. Throw it in the bin, so that nobody else is tempted to use it.

    3. A thief goes through the recycling bins at a block of flats and finds a letter showing a resident’s name, address and account number. Using those details, the thief opens an online buy-now-pay-later account in her name. Which statement is correct?

      • A. Going through the bins was the technique; opening the account was identity theft.
      • B. Going through the bins was identity theft, and opening the account was the technique.
      • C. Both steps were phishing, because personal details were taken.
      • D. Both steps were pretexting, because the thief pretended to be the resident.
    1. B. The stranger never touched the computer. They only watched. Good counters are to angle the screen away and to lock it when you leave. Tailgating is following someone through a door, baiting uses a tempting item, and pretexting is a made-up story.
    2. B. This is baiting by post: a tempting offer is used to get someone to plug a device in. IT can check it safely and look into who sent it. Plugging it into a spare computer is still a risk, and harmful software can run as soon as the drive is plugged in. Binning it keeps colleagues safe, but the attempt then goes unreported.
    3. A. Bin raiding is how the details were obtained. Identity theft is the outcome: using her details to pretend to be her. Option B has the labels the wrong way round. Phishing is a fake message sent to a person, and pretexting is a made-up story told to a person, and neither happened here.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords or card numbers.

    • Attacks on you and your family. Criminals use direct access, identity theft, phishing and social engineering. Which of these have you, or your family, seen attempted? You do not have to share details. Think about what the attempt looked like, whether it worked, and what stopped it, or what would have stopped it. After this episode, which one human defence would you start using first, and what makes that one easy or hard for you?

    You can write only what you are comfortable with, or write “I would rather not say” and move on. If your own identity or card has been misused, contact your bank or card provider straight away, using the number on your card or in their official app. IDCARE is Australia’s national identity and cyber incident support service.

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: match attacks to defences 15, Mateo 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Learners can do both challenges on the same sheet.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners choose “report it” as the first defence for everything. Ask “what stops the attack happening in the first place?”
    • Learners put a technology fix (a filter, a lock) in the matrix. Remind them that the columns are habits.
    • Learners mix up identity theft and the techniques. Use the bin-raiding example: the bin is how, identity theft is what the criminal achieves.
    • Learners feel it is rude to challenge a visitor. Practise the sentence “Can I help you find someone?” out loud.
    • Learners think espionage is only about governments. Mention the small supplier who is a way into a bigger firm.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The prompt asks about attempts on learners or their families, so do not ask anyone to tell a story. Invite people to share only the defence they would start using first. Keep the IDCARE link visible.

    Tip. If you are short of time, run the matrix as a pair activity and go through the primary column together before the backups.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Protect yourself gives plain-language advice on staying safe online.
    • IDCARE is Australia and New Zealand’s national identity and cyber support service. Its site explains what to do if your identity has been misused.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 3 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • Direct access means reaching a device, room or paper in person: tailgating, shoulder surfing, walk-up access, baiting and bin raiding. The best defences are habits: challenge, lock, never plug in, shred.
    • Phishing and pretexting use urgency, authority and trust. The human defence is pause, verify through a channel you already trust, and report with no blame.
    • Identity theft is an outcome. Account takeover with a reused password is one technique that can lead to it.
    • No single defence is enough. Technology and people work as layers, and people are often the last layer.
    • Espionage, bribed insiders and phishing all use human weaknesses, so the same human defences apply.

    References

    Button, M. (2020) ‘Editorial: economic and industrial espionage’, Security Journal, 33(1), pp. 1–5. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1057/s41284-019-00195-5.

    Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Protect yourself. Available at: https://www.cyber.gov.au/protect-yourself (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    IDCARE (n.d.) IDCARE. Available at: https://www.idcare.org (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Privacy and privacy impact assessments

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 58 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is information privacy, what harms follow when it fails, and who is responsible for it?
    • What makes a response to a privacy problem both ethical and practical?
    • What is a privacy impact assessment, and how does a quick threshold assessment decide whether a project needs one?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • explain what information privacy is, and who is responsible for it (ULO 3)
    • describe privacy harms at the individual, group and organisational level, and give an ethical and a practical response (ULO 3)
    • explain what a privacy impact assessment (PIA) is and name its ten steps (ULO 3)
    • apply a threshold assessment to decide whether a project needs a full PIA (ULO 3)

    This episode matches Week 3 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Attack techniques and human defences. That episode was about how attackers get in. This one turns to the other side of the coin: privacy, and how an organisation can check a new project before it puts people’s information at risk.

    What is privacy?

    Privacy has several meanings. In this course we mean information privacy: your ability to know what personal information is collected about you, how it is used and who it is shared with, and to have a say.

    Personal information is anything that identifies you or could reasonably identify you. Some of it is sensitive, such as health information, and needs more care.

    Privacy harms

    Privacy is not just a feeling. When it fails, real harms follow.

    • Money lost through fraud.
    • Identity stolen, as you saw in Identity, identity management and identity theft.
    • Embarrassment or unfair treatment, if private information such as a health condition becomes known.
    • Risk of being found by someone dangerous.
    • Lost trust and control, because you cannot take information back once it is out.

    Harms spread, using the three levels from Digital lives. One person’s exposed health information is an individual harm. A family or team who now doubt each other’s messages is a group harm. An organisation facing complaints, costs and lost trust is an organisational harm. Often one leads to the next.

    Who is responsible?

    Organisations that collect your information carry most of the duty. But you carry some too.

    • Think before you post.
    • Share only what a service needs. A running app does not need your contacts or photos.
    • Check your settings.
    • At work, treat other people’s information with the care you would want for your own.

    An ethical response and a practical response

    When privacy goes wrong, how should an organisation respond? Think about two things.

    • An ethical response asks who is affected and how, and what would be fair to them. It usually means being honest, reducing harm and putting people’s interests alongside the organisation’s.
    • A practical response asks what the organisation can actually do, who will do it, by when, and how it will check that it worked. A tiny charity cannot copy what a bank does.

    The best answer is both, and the two should not contradict each other. It also helps to compare two options. Suppose a business leaks customer emails. It could quietly fix the fault and say nothing, or tell customers and explain how to protect themselves. Telling people costs more at first, but it respects them and lets them act. Say which you would choose, and why. You do not need to invent costs. Say who does the work, when, and why it suits the size of the organisation.

    Privacy impact assessments

    A privacy impact assessment (PIA) is a structured review of a project. It asks how the project could affect people’s privacy, and how to avoid or reduce those effects. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, or OAIC, publishes a free guide (OAIC 2021). Doing a PIA early helps a project meet the law, saves the cost of fixing mistakes later, and shows people that their privacy was considered.

    The threshold assessment

    Not every project needs the same depth. So the OAIC’s first step is a threshold assessment: a quick check, usually short, that you write down. It starts with a simple question. Will any personal information be collected, stored, used or disclosed? If not, a PIA is unlikely to be needed.

    If the answer is yes, you look at how sensitive the information is, what it will be used for, what is changing in how information is handled, and what the people affected might think. You then record whether you will do a full PIA, and who made that decision.

    The OAIC strongly encourages organisations to do PIAs for projects that involve personal information. The legal duty to do one for high privacy risk projects applies to Australian Government agencies, but the idea suits any organisation.

    The ten steps

    If the answer is yes, the guide sets out ten steps:

    1. Threshold assessment
    2. Plan the PIA
    3. Describe the project
    4. Identify and consult stakeholders
    5. Map information flows
    6. Analyse the privacy impacts and check compliance
    7. Manage the risks
    8. Make recommendations
    9. Write a report
    10. Respond and review

    Two are worth a note now. Mapping information flows means tracing where information comes from, where it is kept and who receives it. Recommendations should say who should act and by when. The OAIC guide in Go deeper covers all ten steps.

    Try it on Riverbend

    The first challenge below uses Riverbend Community Library, a made-up library. Read that page once before you start. It describes how the library works. It does not tell you what is right or wrong with it.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Does Riverbend’s new app need a full PIA? (20 minutes)

    Before an organisation starts a big privacy review, it makes a threshold assessment. Here you do that check for a project at Riverbend.

    The project. The library manager has proposed a new Riverbend member app. It would be built and hosted by an outside software company. Members could log in to see what they have borrowed and renew books. The app would suggest books based on each member’s borrowing history. Carers could also sign their children up for the weekend children’s sessions in the app, entering the same details the library holds now: the child’s name, age, carer contact details, allergies and photo consent. The proposal has not been approved yet.

    Use the Riverbend page for the facts about the library. If you need a detail that is not there, say what you are assuming.

    The threshold questions. The OAIC guide sets out a threshold assessment, but not as a numbered list. These six questions put its points in our own words. Questions 1 to 5 follow the guide. Question 6 is added by this lesson.

    # Question
    1 Personal information: will the project collect, store, use or share information about identifiable people? What kinds?
    2 Sensitivity: is any of it especially sensitive, such as health information? Are the people involved children or others who may need extra care?
    3 Purposes: what is the information being collected and used for?
    4 Change: is something new about how the information is collected, stored, used or shared (for example new technology or a new organisation involved)?
    5 Stakeholders: who is affected, and does the scenario show that their views have been asked for?
    6 Scale and handling (added by this lesson): roughly how many people are affected, and who else will handle the information?
    1. Read the Riverbend page (3 minutes).
    2. Answer the six questions (10 minutes). For each, write one or two sentences and point to a detail in the scenario.
    3. Make the decision (7 minutes). Write:
      • one of: “Full PIA needed”, “No full PIA needed” or “Not sure”;
      • two or three reasons, using your answers above;
      • who should be responsible for the PIA at the library and when you would suggest it starts. Use only roles named on the Riverbend page, or say you are assuming one.

    One worked answer. Different learners will notice different details, and that is fine if each one points to something in the scenario.

    # Worked answer
    1 Yes. The app would handle each member’s name, address, date of birth, contact details and borrowing history, and children’s names, ages, carers’ contact details, allergies and photo consent. The Riverbend page lists these under “The information it holds”.
    2 Some of it is sensitive, and some of the people are children. A borrowing history can show what a person is interested in or worried about, and a long history can hint at health, beliefs or family circumstances. Allergies are health information, and they belong to children. Concession status can point to a person’s finances.
    3 Running the library and, in part, suggesting books. Loans, renewals and children’s sign-up fit the library’s purpose. Suggestions use borrowing history in a new way. The scenario does not say whether or how members would be told about this use. That is something the assessment must find out, and a full PIA would examine it.
    4 Yes, a lot is new. The information would be collected through a new app, and an outside company would build and host it. Member and children’s details would sit on that company’s systems, not only on the library’s own. The library has less direct control over them.
    5 Members, carers and children, volunteers and staff, the council and the outside company. The scenario does not say whether members, carers or the volunteers who help at the desk would be asked for their views. The assessment must find that out. The council runs the library and supplies the network, so it is also a stakeholder.
    6 Probably many people, and another organisation handles the data. The page does not give a number of members, so state an assumption, such as “most households in a regional town”. The outside company would handle information as well as the library.

    Decision: Full PIA needed.

    Why (example):

    1. The information is detailed and some of it is sensitive. Borrowing history, allergies and concession status could cause harm if exposed or misused. A threshold assessment cannot settle that. A full PIA can look at each use in turn.
    2. Children are involved. Carers sign children up, and children may not understand how their information is used.
    3. The project is new and involves an outside company. A new app and a new vendor mean new places where information can go, and less control over them. A full PIA would map where information goes.
    4. It has not been approved yet. That is the best time to do the assessment. Changes are cheapest before anything is built or any member’s details are shared.

    Responsible person and time frame (example): the Riverbend page says the library manager and the senior staff make day-to-day decisions about how the library runs, so the library manager could be responsible for the PIA, with the senior staff. The council runs the library, so it is sensible to involve whoever handles privacy at the council. The page does not name that person, so say you are assuming one. The PIA should start before the library commits to the outside company.

    A note on “required” and “recommended”. The OAIC guide says it encourages organisations to do PIAs for projects that involve personal information, and that the legal requirement for “high privacy risk projects” applies to Australian Government agencies (OAIC 2021). So do not rest the decision on that rule. The reasons come from the project: sensitive information, children, a new vendor and a lot of people.

    What counts as correct. Your conclusion should be “Full PIA needed”. “No full PIA needed” and “Not sure” do not fit, because the proposal involves sensitive information, children and an outside company. Do not be concerned if you have fewer reasons than the worked answer.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Deciding because the library is small or volunteer-run. The threshold depends on the information and the project, not on the size of the organisation.
    • Stopping at “yes, personal information is involved”. That only starts the check. Sensitivity, change and scale then decide how deep to go.
    • Using facts that are not in the scenario. Use the Riverbend page and the proposal above. If you need another fact, say that it is an assumption. “A full PIA would check this” is a good sentence.
    • Trying to solve the problems now. A threshold assessment decides whether to do a PIA. It does not find and fix every risk. That is the work of the full PIA.
    • Naming people who are not in the scenario. Choose an owner from the roles on the Riverbend page, or say you are assuming one.
    • Writing “it depends” and stopping. Choose one of the three outcomes and give reasons.
    Challenge

    Challenge: Two ways to respond (8 minutes)

    A fictional scenario. A volunteer-run community swimming club keeps its registration list in an online spreadsheet. Someone shares the link in a group chat so that anyone with the link can open it. The list has members’ names, email addresses and the ages of their children. A parent tells the club president that she opened it by accident.

    1. Name one privacy harm that could follow, and say whether it is an individual, group or organisational harm (2 minutes).
    2. Compare two options (3 minutes): quietly lock the spreadsheet and say nothing, or lock it and tell the members. Which would you choose, and why? Name who is affected and how.
    3. Write a practical response (3 minutes): one action, who does it, by when, and one way to check it worked. Do not invent costs. It must suit a small volunteer club.

    One worked answer.

    1. Harm. Strangers who open the link could use the email addresses to send scams that look real, because they know the person is a swimming club member. That is an individual harm. For the club as an organisation, the harm is lost trust: members may leave or stop volunteering if they feel the club did not look after their details.
    2. Ethical response. Locking and telling is the better choice. Members are the ones affected, and only they can act, for example by treating unexpected emails with care. Saying nothing protects the club’s image but takes that choice away from them. Telling people costs more discomfort at first, but it respects them.
    3. Practical response. The president locks the spreadsheet today so that only named committee members can open it, then emails members this week to explain what happened and what to watch for. At the next committee meeting, one committee member checks who has access. This suits a small volunteer club because it relies on a few people’s time, not on new software.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Thandi downloads a fitness app to log her runs. It asks for access to her contacts, location and photos. Which action shows her taking responsibility for her own privacy?

      • A. Accepting every request so the app works properly.
      • B. Allowing only what the app needs to log runs, then checking her settings.
      • C. Trusting the app store to have decided that sharing her data is safe.
      • D. Deleting the app after one use, whatever the settings.

    2. A school plans an app for a camp. It would record each student’s full medical history, home address and photo, although the camp only needs emergency contacts and allergies. After a threshold assessment, what should the school do?

      • A. Skip a PIA, because it is a one-off camp.
      • B. Carry out a full PIA.
      • C. Do a PIA only after the camp, once parents complain.
      • D. Carry on, because parents will sign a consent form.

    3. A bookshop plans to count how many people enter on each day, using a door sensor that records only totals. Hamish does a threshold assessment and decides that no full PIA is needed because no personal information is involved. What else should he do?

      • A. Record the project, why no full PIA is needed and who made the decision.
      • B. Nothing, as an assessment with a “no” result does not need to be written down.
      • C. Start a full PIA anyway, to be on the safe side.
      • D. Ask a lawyer to sign off the decision before the project goes ahead.
    1. B. Logging runs does not need her contacts or photos, so she should share only what the service needs and check her settings afterwards. Accepting everything gives away more than the service needs. Trusting the app store hands her responsibility to someone else. Deleting the app after one use does not address what she allowed.
    2. B. The app would collect sensitive information about children, and more of it than the camp needs, so a full PIA is warranted. A one-off camp is still a project that handles personal information. Waiting for complaints is too late. A consent form does not replace checking whether so much information is needed.
    3. A. The guide says to keep a record of the threshold assessment, including the project description, whether personal information is involved, the decision and who made it. A “no” is still a decision, and writing it down shows the question was asked and answered. A full PIA is unlikely to be needed for a project with no personal information, and the guide does not call for outside sign-off.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords, card numbers or account details.

    • What privacy means to you. What is data privacy? In your own words, what does it mean to you? Think about one piece of personal information you would never want shared (for example your health, your location or your messages) and why. Who do you think is responsible for protecting it: you, the organisations that hold it, or both? Is there anything you share online that you would now think twice about?

    Timing (58 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 38 minutes: Riverbend threshold assessment 20, two ways to respond 8, quick check 5, discussion 5. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 3 minutes at the start of the first challenge.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think a PIA is only for big projects or big organisations. Ask what a small library would lose if the app leaked children’s allergies.
    • Learners treat “yes, personal information is involved” as the answer. Ask what happens next in the threshold assessment.
    • Learners start fixing the app’s risks. Remind them that the threshold assessment only decides whether to do a PIA.
    • Learners add facts to Riverbend, such as the number of members. Ask them to say “I am assuming”.
    • Learners say “it depends”. Ask them to choose one of the three outcomes and give reasons.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The question about information learners would never want shared can be personal, so ask pairs to share the reason and not the information itself. The answer “both of us” to “who is responsible” is usually correct, so ask what each party’s part is.

    Tip. Collect the pairs’ reasons for the Riverbend decision on a board, then group them by sensitivity, children, new technology and the outside company. Ask which reason is strongest.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (2021) Guide to undertaking privacy impact assessments is free to read. It is long, so start with the introduction and the threshold assessment, then skim the openings of steps 2 to 10.
    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.) Privacy impact assessments is the OAIC’s overview page for PIAs.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 3 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • Information privacy means knowing what is collected about you, how it is used and who it is shared with, and having a say.
    • When privacy fails, harms follow: lost money, stolen identity, embarrassment or unfair treatment, risk of being found, and lost trust. They spread from individuals to groups and organisations.
    • Organisations carry most of the duty for privacy, but individuals carry some: share only what a service needs, and care for other people’s information.
    • A good response is both ethical (who is affected, what is fair) and practical (who does what, by when, and how it is checked).
    • A threshold assessment is a quick, written check that decides whether a project needs a full PIA. Sensitivity, children, new technology and outside companies all point towards a full PIA.

    References

    Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) (2021) Guide to undertaking privacy impact assessments, 2 September. Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/privacy-impact-assessments/guide-to-undertaking-privacy-impact-assessments (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.) Privacy impact assessments. Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/privacy-guidance-for-organisations-and-government-agencies/privacy-impact-assessments (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Social media and what attackers can build from it

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How can a public social media profile be joined up and used against its owner?
    • How does social software lead to fake accounts, hijacked accounts and personal attacks?
    • What can you do to share what you want while giving away less?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • explain how a public social media profile can be joined up and misused (ULO 1, ULO 3)
    • describe how social software leads to fake accounts, hijacked accounts and personal attacks, and what to do about them (ULO 1, ULO 3)
    • recommend practical steps that cut down what a profile gives away (ULO 3)

    This episode matches Week 4 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Privacy and privacy impact assessments. That episode looked at privacy from the organisation’s side. This one looks at the information people hand out themselves. The second half of the week is in the next episode, People at work: BYOD and working from home.

    Callout

    Content note

    This episode mentions online harassment, impersonation and the publishing of someone’s home address (doxxing), in general terms. It describes no real person. If that is close to something that has happened to you, you can skim those parts. In the second challenge, you can skip the personal-attack option and choose another.

    Your profile is a puzzle

    One post is rarely dangerous. A whole profile is different, because an attacker can lay the pieces side by side. In Social engineering: hacking the human you met the research stage of an attack, where the attacker quietly collects facts. Social media is a very good research tool for a criminal, and we fill it in ourselves, for free.

    Think about what a public profile can show.

    • Facts: your name, your suburb, where you work.
    • Patterns: when you post from the gym, or which café you visit on Fridays.
    • Relationships: who your family, friends and manager are.
    • Feelings: whether you are happy at work or fed up.
    • Answers: details that sound like the answers to security questions, such as a first pet or a first school.

    Each piece looks harmless. Together, they let someone write a message that sounds as if it came from your manager, guess how to reset your password, or work out when your house is empty.

    You are not the only one who decides what appears. Other people post about you. A friend tags you at a party, a club posts a group photo, a colleague mentions where you work. The National Cyber Security Centre in the United Kingdom, the NCSC, advises you to be aware of what others say about you online, because criminals can use it for identity theft or more convincing phishing (NCSC 2022). The same goes for what you post about others: check with them first.

    What you can do

    • Check who can see your posts, and share only what is needed. Most platforms let you choose between everyone, friends or a smaller group. The NCSC advises managing your security and privacy settings (NCSC 2022).
    • Turn on two-step verification. It asks for a second proof when you log in, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough. It is the same idea as multi-factor authentication in Identity, identity management and identity theft.
    • Think about your digital footprint. That is the trail of information about you that exists online, including what other people post about you.
    • Ask before you post: could a stranger use this?

    Fakes, hijacks and personal attacks

    Fake accounts

    Social software makes it easy to pretend. The NCSC suggests checking when an account was set up, whether the name looks random, and whether the follower count fits, because followers can be bought. It adds that verification badges can help you identify real accounts (NCSC 2022). If you are not sure, do not accept the request, and use the platform’s report button.

    Hijacked accounts

    A real friend’s account can also be taken over. If a contact suddenly posts something out of character, the NCSC advises checking with them by another method, such as a phone call, in case the account was hacked (NCSC 2022). Do not ask in the same chat. That is where the attacker is waiting, and they may answer.

    Personal attacks

    Then there are attacks on people.

    • Online harassment is repeated, unwanted or abusive behaviour aimed at a person.
    • Impersonation is someone posting as you to damage your name.
    • Doxxing is collecting a person’s private details, such as a home address or workplace, and publishing them so that others can find them. It often starts with the same joining of small pieces you have just read about.

    The harm is real: fear, lost sleep, and sometimes a person no longer feels safe at home.

    If it happens to you, a few steps help.

    1. Do not argue with the attackers.
    2. Save evidence, such as screenshots showing dates and usernames.
    3. Report the posts to the platform.
    4. Tell someone you trust, and tell your employer if work is involved.
    5. If someone is impersonating you, warn the people who might be fooled, using your real account.

    In Australia, the eSafety Commissioner provides information on reporting serious online abuse (eSafety Commissioner n.d.). If you feel physically threatened, contact the police. If you see it happening to someone else, do not share it or pile on. Report it, and check in with the person.

    Try it on a fictional profile

    The first two challenges use one fictional profile. Everything in it is invented. Jonty Pell is not a real person, and the town, the employer, the software, the street and the people are all made up. Do not use this as a reason to look up a real person. Never build a picture of a real colleague, friend or stranger from their profile.

    Challenge

    Challenge: What does the profile show? (12 minutes)

    The profile. Jonty Pell (fictional). Bio: “Numbers by day, sourdough by night. Marrow Creek. Dog dad to Biscuit. Bookkeeper at Greywater Timber Supplies. Marrow Creek High, class of 2014.” The profile is public. Anyone can see it.

    # Post Date
    1 “Turning 30 on the 14th! Drinks at the Railway Hotel, Saturday 6 pm, all welcome.” 3 Nov
    2 “Month-end again. Payroll goes out Thursday and I’m the only one who knows the bank portal. Denise says no pressure. Ha.” 5 Nov
    3 Check-in: “Marrow Creek Fitness, 6:10 am. Monday, Wednesday and Friday regulars, you know who you are.” 7 Nov
    4 “Twelve days in Portugal! Flying out Friday. The house will be empty, ha. Biscuit is off to my sister Bree’s.” 9 Nov
    5 “Throwback to Gerald, my first car, a yellow 2004 Corolla. And Pepper, my first ever pet, a very grumpy cat.” 11 Nov
    6 “Happy birthday to my mum, Linda Pell (née Ferris)! Love you.” 12 Nov
    7 “Third change to the invoice process this term. LedgerLark is driving me up the wall.” 14 Nov
    8 “Passed over for supervisor again. Maybe it’s time for something new.” 16 Nov
    9 Photo of a freshly painted door: “Finally painted the front door at no. 14! Wattle Street’s sunniest door.” 18 Nov
    10 Photo tagged by a colleague: “Greywater Timber team night out. Thanks Denise Halloran for dinner!” 20 Nov
    1. Read the profile (2 minutes).
    2. List what it states (4 minutes). Write at least eight things the profile says outright, with the post number for each.
    3. Join the pieces (6 minutes). Write at least three things an attacker could work out by joining two or more items. For each, say which post numbers you joined. Use “could” or “may” for anything the profile does not say outright.

    One worked answer. Yours may differ.

    Stated (at least eight needed). His name, town and job as a bookkeeper at Greywater Timber Supplies (bio). His school and the year he finished, 2014 (bio). That he turns 30 on the 14th, with the party venue and time (post 1). That he is the only one who knows the payroll bank portal, that payroll goes out on Thursday, and that someone called Denise has told him there is no pressure (post 2). That he is at Marrow Creek Fitness at 6:10 am on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays (post 3). That he is away for 12 days from a Friday, that the house will be empty and that his dog is with his sister Bree (post 4). His first car and first pet (post 5). His mother’s name and maiden name (post 6). The software his employer uses, LedgerLark, and his frustration with it (post 7). That he was passed over for supervisor (post 8). His house number and street (post 9). The full name of a colleague, Denise Halloran (post 10; the posts do not say whether she is his manager).

    What an attacker could work out (at least three needed).

    What an attacker could work out Posts joined
    His approximate year of birth Bio (class of 2014) and post 1 (turning 30)
    His street address: no. 14 Wattle Street, Marrow Creek Post 9 (number and street) and the bio (town)
    That the house at that address will be empty for 12 days from the Friday Posts 4 and 9
    That he has a set early-morning routine, so he is out on those days Post 3
    That a fake payroll message that appears to come from a colleague, such as Denise Halloran, could fit his real week Posts 2 and 10 (and 7 for the software name)
    That he may be open to a job offer Posts 7 and 8
    Possible answers to account-recovery questions: first pet (Pepper), first car (a yellow 2004 Corolla), mother’s maiden name (Ferris), school Bio, posts 5 and 6

    The profile does not say whether he lives alone, whether anyone else is in the house, or what his bank or email providers are. Any statement about those would be a guess, so a good answer says “could” or leaves them out.

    Challenge

    Challenge: How could it be misused, and how do you protect it? (13 minutes)

    Use Jonty’s profile from the previous challenge.

    1. Show how it could be misused (9 minutes). Choose three of these misuse types, one row each:
        1. guessing the answers to account-recovery questions, or guessing passwords;
      • (b) writing a convincing fake message to Jonty or his workplace;
      • (c) a real-world risk, such as to Jonty’s home or belongings;
      • (d) approaching Jonty with a believable offer or story;
      • (e) a personal attack, such as harassment or publishing his address (skip this one if you would rather).
      For each, write what the attacker would do, which post numbers they would join (at least two), and who could be hurt.
    2. Say how to protect it (4 minutes). Write three changes Jonty could make, and one thing Greywater Timber Supplies could do to help its staff.

    One worked answer. Any three misuse types that you can support with two or more post numbers are sound.

    Type What the attacker would do Posts joined Who could be hurt
    (a) Recovery answers If Jonty’s accounts use questions such as “first pet” or “mother’s maiden name”, try Pepper, Gerald or Ferris, and use his birthday and school to guess passwords. Then take over an account. Bio, 1, 5, 6 Jonty (his accounts), and anyone who trusts messages from them
    (b) Fake message Send Jonty an email that appears to come from Denise Halloran (who could be a colleague or manager; the posts do not say), saying “payroll is urgent, please change this staff member’s bank account in LedgerLark today”. Jonty says he is the only one who knows the portal, so a fake request could seem to fit his real week. 2, 7, 10 Staff, who might be paid wrongly; Greywater, which could lose money; Jonty, who may be blamed
    (c) Real world Know that the house at no. 14 Wattle Street, Marrow Creek, will be empty for 12 days from a Friday. 4, 9, bio Jonty (his belongings and his home)
    (d) Believable offer Contact him as a “recruiter” with a story about a better job, knowing he feels passed over. The attacker could ask him for documents “to apply”, or for access. 7, 8 Jonty and Greywater, if he shares work information
    (e) Personal attack Collect his address and workplace and publish them to harass him, which is doxxing. Someone angry about something at his workplace could do this. 9, 10, bio Jonty, his family and his colleagues, who may feel unsafe

    Protection.

    • Jonty could: set his posts to friends only; post holiday photos after he is home; leave out his street and house number; not post answers that sound like security questions (first pet, first car, mother’s maiden name); keep complaints about work for a private talk with his manager; ask colleagues to check before tagging him.
    • Greywater could: give staff short, specific rules on what not to share (for example payroll roles, software names and anything confidential), explain the reasons, and make it easy to ask questions. A second person should approve any change to payroll details, so one fake message cannot move money. This links to two-person approval in The insider threat.
    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Listing facts only. The point is the joining. “He goes to the gym” is a fact. “He is out of the house at 6 am on set days” is what an attacker could work out.
    • Stating guesses as facts. The profile does not say whether Jonty lives alone or which bank he uses. Write “could” or “may” for what is not stated.
    • Citing only one post. A misuse that uses one post is not a profile puzzle. Join at least two.
    • Blaming Jonty. He is an ordinary person sharing normal life. Say what could be done to reduce the risk, not that he was foolish.
    • Choosing only technical attacks. The profile gives an attacker facts about people. Most of the misuse is about believable stories and guesses, not hacking.
    • “He should delete everything.” A good answer keeps what is useful about sharing and changes who sees it, when and how much.
    • Using a real profile. Do not practise on a real person, even if their posts are public.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Zainab shares photos of her weekend hikes with a few close friends, but her profile is set to public. Which step best reduces what a stranger can learn about her, while she keeps posting?

      • A. Turn off comments on her photos.
      • B. Change the audience to friends only, and check who is on that list.
      • C. Take photos without her face in them.
      • D. Rely on the platform to hide anything private.

    2. Sunita gets a connection request on a professional networking site from someone who says they supply her company’s printers. The profile was set up last week, its name is a random string of letters, and it has thousands of followers but no posts. What does this most clearly show?

      • A. A new account, a random-looking name and a follower count that does not fit.
      • B. A verification badge and a long work history.
      • C. A friendly photo and a polite message.
      • D. A shared connection and a company logo.

    3. Brendan belongs to a cycling club’s group chat. A fellow member’s account suddenly posts a link with the message “Is this you in this video??”. The member has never posted anything like this before. What is the best response?

      • A. Click the link quickly, to see if the video shows him.
      • B. Reply in the group chat and ask whether the account has been hacked.
      • C. Leave the link alone, and contact the member another way, such as by phone.
      • D. Forward the link on to the other members, so they can say whether it is safe.
    1. B. Settings decide who can see a post. Turning off comments, hiding her face or relying on the platform’s defaults does not change the audience.
    2. A. These are the things the NCSC suggests checking, and together they suggest a fake account. A verification badge, a friendly message or a shared logo would point the other way, and a polite message proves nothing.
    3. C. A link from a hijacked account is the attacker’s way in, so do not click it. The NCSC advises checking with a contact by another method if they post something out of character, in case their account was hacked. Asking in the group chat may reach the attacker, who may even answer. Forwarding the link spreads the risk to more people.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords, card numbers, account details or your address. If any of this is close to something that has happened to you, write only what you are comfortable with.

    • Social media and your own information. Do you think social media is really safe? What makes you say that? How do you protect your own personal data online, and is there one habit you would change after this episode? Why do people share personal information, for example on Instagram, even when they know the risks? Think about what you get from sharing, and what it might cost you. Some countries control which social media their people can use. What do you think of that: when might it protect people, and when might it harm them?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: what the profile shows 12, misuse and protection 13, quick check 5, discussion 5.

    Content note. Say at the start that the episode mentions harassment and doxxing in general terms. Tell learners that skipping option (e) is fine. Do not ask anyone to share personal experiences. If a learner is upset, point them to the eSafety Commissioner and, in your own setting, to your usual support.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners list facts and stop. Ask them to point to two posts and say what the pair shows that neither shows alone.
    • Learners write guesses as facts, such as “he lives alone”. Ask where the profile says it, and show them “could”.
    • Learners blame Jonty. Ask what a reasonable person would think about a birthday post.
    • Learners suggest “delete everything”. Ask what Jonty would lose, and whether a smaller audience would do.
    • Learners want to look up a real person to make the task “realistic”. Say no, and explain that profiling a real person is not an acceptable practice exercise.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The prompt asks about personal habits, so ask pairs to share the reason behind a habit and not the details of their accounts. The last question, about why people share despite the risks, tends to produce the best talk: ask what each reason gets the sharer and who pays the cost. For the question about countries that control social media, ask who decides what “protect” means.

    Tip. Run the profile challenge with sticky notes. Give each pair ten post numbers on a board and ask them to draw lines between posts that join. The pattern of lines shows how much more a pair says than a single post.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • National Cyber Security Centre (2022) Social media: how to use it safely is a short page for the general public. It covers privacy settings, two-step verification, your digital footprint and spotting fake accounts.
    • eSafety Commissioner (n.d.) Report online harm is the Australian page for reporting serious online abuse.

    The NCSC is a United Kingdom body. The Australian Cyber Security Centre is the local equivalent.

    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 4 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • One post is a piece. A whole profile is the picture, and an attacker can join facts, patterns, relationships, feelings and answers to build a believable story.
    • Other people’s posts about you count too, so check before you post about them.
    • Cut down what a profile gives away: choose the audience, share only what is needed, use two-step verification, and think about who could use a post.
    • Check a suspect account’s age, name and follower count. If a friend’s account acts oddly, check with them another way, not in the same chat.
    • If you are attacked online: do not argue, save evidence, report, tell someone, and warn others if you are being impersonated.

    References

    National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) (2022) Social media: how to use it safely, 5 September. Available at: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/social-media-how-to-use-it-safely (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    eSafety Commissioner (n.d.) Report online harm. Available at: https://www.esafety.gov.au/report (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from People at work: BYOD and working from home

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How should an organisation manage people, including unhappy staff, social media use and its own control over staff?
    • What does a security rule gain, and what does it cost the people who must follow it?
    • What are the risks and sensible controls for staff using their own devices, or working away from the office?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • describe how an organisation can manage people, including unhappy staff, social media use and employer control, in a fair and effective way (ULO 1)
    • apply three tests (proportionate, open, about work) to an employer’s control over staff (ULO 1, ULO 3)
    • weigh the security a BYOD or work-from-home rule gains against the burden it puts on staff (ULO 1, ULO 3)

    This episode matches Week 4 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Social media and what attackers can build from it, which looked at what people give away on their own time. This one looks at the workplace: how an organisation treats its people, and what its rules cost them.

    People are part of the defence

    In The insider threat you met Colwill (2009), who writes about the insider threat. His abstract says that technical controls must not be used in isolation, and that questions of loyalty arise when an organisation is going through change. This episode takes the same paper’s concern, the people side of security, into everyday workplace questions.

    Social media at work

    Social media at work raises three people questions.

    • What may staff say about the organisation?
    • What must they not share?
    • What happens when someone is unhappy?

    A rule that says only “never post about work” is hard to follow and easy to ignore. Better guidance is specific. Do not share customer details. Do not share anything confidential. And here is who to ask if you are not sure. Explain the reasons, train people, and make it safe to say, “I made a mistake.” The NCSC has a page for organisations on protecting what they publish, which is listed under Go deeper below.

    Unhappy staff and change

    When someone is unhappy, or the organisation is changing, the risk goes up. A staff member who feels ignored may post a complaint online, or worse, take information with them. Managers who notice, listen and treat people fairly lower that risk far more than any filter can. A filter does not deal with why the person is upset.

    What an employer may reasonably do

    Employers have a legitimate interest. They own the work systems, and they are responsible for the information on them. So it is reasonable for an employer to set rules for work computers, and to log activity on them. The test has three parts.

    1. Proportionate. Is the control in proportion to the risk?
    2. Open. Are staff told what is watched, and why?
    3. About work. Does it stay focused on work?

    An employer who secretly reads private messages, or demands the passwords to your personal accounts, has gone past that test. Staff have duties too: follow the rules, report problems early, and think before you post.

    What tighter security costs

    Every control costs someone something. Passwords that expire weekly, approval for every app, a ban on personal phones. Each can make the organisation safer, and each can make work slower. When the cost is too high, people find workarounds. They email files to themselves, use free apps nobody approved, or leave sessions open. A control that people go around can be worse than none, because the organisation believes it is protected.

    So ask two questions of any rule.

    • How much security does it add?
    • How much burden does it put on staff?

    Good policy keeps the first high and the second low. In the first challenge you will score rules on both.

    BYOD: bring your own device

    BYOD stands for bring your own device. Staff use their own phones or laptops for work. The benefits are lower cost and familiar tools. The risks are these.

    • Personal and work data mix.
    • The device can be lost.
    • It may be too old to receive security updates.
    • Work files may copy into a personal cloud account.
    • The organisation does not own the device, so it cannot simply inspect or wipe it.

    Sensible controls include a screen lock and encryption, an approved list of devices that still receive updates, and keeping work data in a separate work app or profile. Then a lost phone can have the work data removed without touching the owner’s personal photos. There should also be a clear rule for when someone leaves: the work accounts and data are removed from the phone, and the owner’s personal data is left alone.

    Volunteers are a special case. They are not employees, and an organisation has less claim on their phones. The same logic applies, only more strongly: ask for as little as the risk needs.

    Working from home or off-site

    The office has managed networks, locked doors and colleagues nearby. At home, the network is yours: perhaps a router still using its default password, and updates that keep getting postponed. In a café, there is public Wi-Fi, and people who can see your screen or hear your calls.

    Useful controls are the organisation’s secure remote access, a private place to work, devices kept up to date, and screens locked when you step away. Your responsibilities are to follow the rules, keep work separate from home life, and report a lost device or an odd message quickly, without fear of blame.

    Try it on Riverbend

    The first two challenges use Riverbend Community Library, a made-up library. Read that page once before you start. It describes how the library works. It does not tell you what is right or wrong with it.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Score Riverbend’s draft rules (15 minutes)

    The situation. Riverbend’s volunteers use their own phones, and the roster is organised through a group chat. This episode adds two details for the exercise. Some paid staff would like to prepare the monthly newsletter at home, using the free online tool that holds the mailing list. The library manager has written two short draft policies, one for each situation. They are drafts only. Nobody has agreed to them.

    Draft 1: Volunteers’ phones and the roster

    # Rule
    1.1 Volunteers may keep using their own phones for the roster. The group chat is for shifts and changes only.
    1.2 Do not put children’s names, allergies or members’ details in the group chat, or in any message or photo on your phone. If you need to pass one on, speak to the library manager or a senior staff member.
    1.3 Every volunteer must install an app chosen by the library. It lets the library see the phone’s apps, messages and location, so the library can check the roster.
    1.4 When a volunteer stops volunteering, the library removes them from the group chat on their last day.

    Draft 2: Working from home

    # Rule
    2.1 Paid staff may prepare the newsletter at home on their own computer, and are expected to install updates promptly.
    2.2 The mailing list may be opened only on a library laptop. Staff collect it at the start of each working day and return it to the library at the end.
    2.3 To sign in to the mailing-list tool, staff enter a code from a phone app as well as their password.
    2.4 If you lose a phone or computer used for library work, tell the library manager as soon as you notice.

    Use the Riverbend page for facts about the library and the drafts above for what each rule says. If you need a detail that neither gives, say what you are assuming.

    1. Read the page and the drafts (3 minutes).

    2. Score every rule (12 minutes). Copy the table below, with 8 rows, one for each rule. Give each rule two scores from 1 to 5:

      • Security gained: 1 = adds very little protection, 5 = adds a lot.
      • Burden on staff or volunteers: 1 = very light, 5 = very heavy.

      Add one short reason for each pair of scores. Only use what the rule says. If it does not say something, do not assume it.

      Rule Security gained (1–5) Burden (1–5) Reason
      1.1

    One worked answer. A score one point higher or lower is sound if your reason fits the rule’s words.

    Rule Security gained Burden Reason
    1.1 2 1 Volunteers carry on as they do now, so the burden is almost nil. Limiting the chat to shifts and changes helps a little, but the rule does not say how this is kept to.
    1.2 4 2 It keeps children’s details and members’ details out of a chat on personal phones. The Riverbend page says the children’s program records allergies and photo consent, so these are details worth keeping out. The cost is a conversation with the manager or a senior staff member when a detail must be passed on.
    1.3 3 5 The library could see everything on a volunteer’s phone, including personal messages and location, which goes far beyond the roster. It is hard to see how this is in proportion to the risk, and it is not just about library work. Volunteers give their time freely, so many might refuse. The rule does not say what the library would do with what it sees.
    1.4 4 1 Removing a person from the chat on their last day cuts off their access to later shifts and changes. The cost is small. The rule does not say what happens to anything already sent to that person’s phone.
    2.1 2 1 Asking staff to install updates is a good habit but checks nothing. There is nothing about a screen lock or about where the mailing list may be kept.
    2.2 4 4 Only library-owned laptops open the list, so a lot less could leak from home computers. But staff must collect and return the laptop every working day, which defeats much of the point of working from home. The rule does not say what staff do if they cannot get to the library.
    2.3 5 2 A second check at each sign-in means a stolen password alone is not enough, for a few seconds at each login. The rule assumes staff have a phone that can run the app.
    2.4 3 1 Quick reporting limits the damage of a loss and costs almost nothing. But the rule only says to tell the manager. It does not say what the library would then do.
    Challenge

    Challenge: Weigh the trade and improve the rules (10 minutes)

    Use your scores from the previous challenge. Write 2 to 4 sentences for each of these.

    1. Worst and best trade (4 minutes). Which rule is the worst trade (a heavy burden for little security gained)? Which is the best trade?
    2. Workarounds (3 minutes). What might staff or volunteers do if a rule’s burden is very high? What would that do to the security gained?
    3. Rewrite (3 minutes). Choose one rule from Draft 1 and one rule from Draft 2. Rewrite each so that the balance improves. Say what you changed and why.

    One worked answer.

    1. Worst and best trade. The worst trade is rule 1.3. It asks volunteers to give the library a view of their phones, and it gains less than it costs. Rule 2.2 is close, because it gains security but takes away most of the benefit of working from home. The best trade is rule 2.3: a code from a phone app costs a few seconds and protects the mailing list even if a password is stolen. Rule 1.2 is also a good trade. Either 2.3 or 1.2 is a sound choice if you say why.
    2. Workarounds. Volunteers might refuse the app, or leave the group chat for another way to swap shifts. Staff might email the mailing list to themselves so they do not have to carry the laptop. Each workaround breaks the protection the rule was meant to give. The library would believe it was protected, and it would not be.
    3. Rewrites (examples).
      • Rule 1.3: “The library sets up a roster app or chat that it manages. Volunteers use that for shifts, and the library can remove a volunteer’s access to it. The library cannot see anything else on a volunteer’s phone.” This keeps the part the library needs, control over its own roster, and removes the part that reaches into personal phones.
      • Rule 2.2: “Staff may open the mailing list at home on a computer that is kept up to date and has a screen lock. They sign in with a password and a code, and do not save the list to the computer.” This asks for a small habit in place of carrying a laptop, and it still protects the list.
      • Rule 2.1: “Staff who work at home keep their computer up to date and use a screen lock.” This is specific, so it is easier to follow and to check.
      • Rule 1.4: “On a volunteer’s last day, the library removes them from the group chat and asks them to delete any library details from their phone.” This closes the gap the rule left open.
      • Any rewrite is sound if it improves the balance and you say why.

    An overall point. Neither draft gets the balance right everywhere. Draft 1 asks little of volunteers in some rules, then asks far too much in one. Draft 2 has a strong, light rule in 2.3, but its strictest rule makes working from home hard. Better policies keep the burden low and the protection high, for example with a separate work app, a small sign-in code and specific, explained rules.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Scoring only the security side. Both scores matter. A strict rule can be a poor trade if the burden is heavy.
    • Thinking strict means safe. A rule that people work around can protect less than a lighter rule that people follow.
    • Thinking light means friendly. A rule that asks almost nothing can still cost staff, members and children a great deal if something goes wrong.
    • Assuming facts that are not in the rule. The drafts do not say how the app would be used, what the library would do after a loss, or how anyone would check the rules. Score what is written, and say “the rule does not say”.
    • Giving a score with no reason. One short reason that points to the rule’s words is enough.
    • Rewriting a rule by deleting it. A better rule keeps the useful part and lowers the burden.
    • Adding facts about Riverbend. Use the Riverbend page and the drafts above. If you need a detail, say it is an assumption.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Odile resigns from her job. She has used her own phone for work email and files. What should the organisation’s policy say happens on her last day?

      • A. Nothing, because she is a trusted former colleague.
      • B. The whole phone is wiped, including her personal photos and messages.
      • C. The work accounts and data are removed from the phone, and her personal data is left alone.
      • D. She is asked to delete the work email app herself within a month.

    2. Emeka’s own tablet is nine years old and no longer receives security updates from its maker. He asks to use it for work email under the company’s BYOD policy. What is the best response?

      • A. Allow it, because it works well and has a screen lock set up.
      • B. Decline it for work and explain why, then offer a supported or loan device instead.
      • C. Allow it for a one-month trial, then review whether it is still safe to use.
      • D. Allow it, as long as he promises not to open any attachments in his work email.

    3. A company asks staff who use their own phones for work to install software that can read all their personal messages and track their location around the clock. What is the best way to handle this?

      • A. Install it on every phone, because the company owns all the work data.
      • B. Install it, and promise to read messages only if someone complains about that particular staff member.
      • C. Allow personal phones only for staff who agree to be tracked by the company during all of their working hours.
      • D. Limit control to a separate work app, tell staff what can be seen, and leave personal data alone.
    1. C. Work data left on a former employee’s device is a risk, and wiping her personal photos would be unfair. Trusting her does not remove the data, and asking her to delete the app within a month leaves the data on the phone for weeks.
    2. B. An approved list should include only devices that still receive security updates, and offering an alternative keeps the burden on Emeka low. A screen lock does not fix known weaknesses that will never be patched. A trial month still leaves work data on a device that cannot be kept up to date. A promise not to open attachments is not a control, because many weaknesses can be reached without opening one.
    3. D. This passes the three tests: it is proportionate, staff are told what is watched and why, and it stays focused on work. Reading all personal messages and tracking location around the clock goes far beyond what protecting work data needs. A promise to read only after a complaint still collects far more than the risk needs.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords, card numbers or account details.

    • Work, devices and control. How much control should an employer have over what you do on a work computer or network? Where would you draw the line, using the three tests (proportionate, open and about work)? Should you have to use your own phone for work? What would make you comfortable, or not, about doing it? Why is working from home, or from somewhere else, harder to secure than working in an office, and what do you think your own responsibilities would be to your employer?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: score Riverbend’s draft rules 15, weigh the trade and improve the rules 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 3 minutes at the start of the first challenge.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think strict means safe. Ask what a volunteer or staff member would do if the rule made the job much harder.
    • Learners think light means friendly. Ask who pays if a lost phone holds children’s allergy details.
    • Learners score only one column. Hold them to both scores and a reason.
    • Learners add facts to Riverbend or to the drafts, such as how the library would use the app. Ask them to say “the rule does not say” or “I am assuming”.
    • Learners rewrite a rule by deleting it. Ask what the library would lose.
    • Learners treat volunteers like employees. Ask what claim an organisation has on a volunteer’s own phone.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share. The question about using your own phone for work is personal, so ask pairs to share the condition that would make them comfortable and not their own phone settings. Ask pairs who disagree about where to draw the line to apply the three tests to the same example.

    Tip. Put the eight rules on a board and ask each pair to place a sticky note for each rule on a grid with security gained across and burden up. The rules in the bottom-right corner (high security, low burden) are the good trades. Discuss the ones in the top-left.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • National Cyber Security Centre (2020) Social media: protecting what you publish is written for organisations. It covers who may publish on an organisation’s social media accounts and what to do if an account is taken over.
    • National Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Device security guidance is a collection of guidance for organisations on how to choose, configure and use devices securely.

    The NCSC is a United Kingdom body. The Australian Cyber Security Centre is the local equivalent.

    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 4 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • People are part of the defence. Technical controls on their own are not enough, and managers who notice, listen and treat people fairly lower the risk more than any filter.
    • Specific, explained social media guidance works better than “never post about work”. Say what not to share and who to ask, and make it safe to admit a mistake.
    • An employer’s control passes the test if it is proportionate to the risk, open to the staff it affects, and about work.
    • Ask two questions of every rule: how much security does it add, and how much burden does it put on people? Rules that are too heavy get worked around.
    • BYOD and working from home need clear rules: updated devices, a separate work app or profile, secure remote access, quick reporting, and removing work data when someone leaves.

    References

    Colwill, C. (2009) ‘Human factors in information security: the insider threat – who can you trust these days?’, Information Security Technical Report, 14(4), pp. 186–196. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.istr.2010.04.004.

    National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) (2020) Social media: protecting what you publish, 30 June. Available at: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/social-media-protect-what-you-publish (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) (n.d.) Device security guidance. Available at: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/device-security-guidance (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Security awareness that changes behaviour

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What makes a security awareness activity change what people do, and not just what they have heard?
    • How can an organisation check that behaviour has really changed?
    • How secure is your own ICT life, and what is one change you can make this week?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • describe an awareness activity that is short, specific, role-based and repeated, with a safe way to report (ULO 2)
    • explain how to check that people changed what they do, and not only that they attended (ULO 2)
    • check your own personal ICT security and choose one change to make (ULO 2)

    This episode matches Week 5 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows People at work: BYOD and working from home. Earlier episodes looked at the risks. From here the course turns to answers, and the answers are about people. The second half of the week is in the next episode, Vetting, trust and access.

    Three things, and each has a limit

    A good plan for the people side of security rests on three things: what staff know, who is let in, and how much any one person can reach. Each has a limit.

    • Awareness. Staff cannot follow rules they have never heard, or rules that are too vague to use. This episode covers it.
    • Vetting. Checking a person before you give them trust tells you about their past, and nothing about their future. The next episode covers it.
    • Access. The more one person can reach, the more damage one mistake or one bad decision can do. The next episode covers this too.

    A good plan uses all three together. We start with awareness.

    Awareness is not the same as a policy

    Awareness means that staff understand what the risks are and what is expected of them. It is not the same as having a policy. A policy can sit in a folder that nobody opens. Awareness shows up in what people do on a busy Tuesday.

    Why does it matter so much? Most people who break a rule are not careless on purpose. They are rushing, or they never knew the rule, or the safe way felt slower and nobody explained why it mattered. Awareness closes that gap. It tells people what the risk is, in plain words, and what you want them to do instead.

    Five things that make awareness work

    Feature What it means
    Short Ten or twenty minutes that people take in beat a two-hour session they sit through.
    Specific Use examples from your own workplace, not a general warning about hackers.
    Role-based A receptionist, an accountant and a manager meet different risks, so each group needs different examples.
    Repeated Starting a new job is the best moment to teach. A short reminder every few months stops it fading. Part-timers, casuals and contractors need it too, because attackers do not check someone’s hours first.
    Safe to report If people fear blame, they hide mistakes. A hidden mistake is a much bigger problem than an admitted one.

    How will you know it worked?

    Counting how many people attended a session only tells you that they sat in a room. Better evidence is about behaviour.

    • Are more suspicious messages being reported?
    • Do spot checks find fewer devices left unlocked?
    • Do fewer people click on a test phishing message?

    Notice that more reports can be a good sign. It can mean people feel safe to speak up, not that more attacks are happening.

    The wider picture

    Bartlett (2018) is the reading for this week. The subtitle of his book gives his argument: that the internet is damaging democracy, and what can be done about it. It is a book about technology and society at large, so it is not a guide to staff training. This episode is where awareness is taught. The reading is useful for one thing here: it asks you to think about trust and power, and about who can see and do what with information. You will use that thinking in the next episode.

    Your own ICT life

    The habits you have at home come with you to work. A phone with no passcode, an old account you forgot, or one password kept in a plain note can become a workplace problem. It is also easier to ask other people to change a habit once you have changed one of your own, because you know how it feels.

    The first challenge asks you to check your own ICT security. It is private.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Check your own ICT security (15 minutes)

    This activity is private. Keep your answers to yourself. Nobody needs to read your list.

    • Never write down, type, photograph or share a password, a PIN, a recovery code or an account number. Not in the checklist, and not with anyone else.
    • Check only your own devices, accounts and home network. Do not check anyone else’s phone or laptop, and do not try to log in to a router, device or account that is not yours.
    • If you share a device with family, check only the parts that belong to you.
    1. Make a list (3 minutes). On paper or in a note on your own device, list what you use in five areas: devices (phones, tablets, laptops, a smart TV, a game console, and any old ones in a drawer), apps and accounts (email, banking, social media, cloud storage, shopping), password storage (where your passwords live), networks (home Wi-Fi, mobile data, public Wi-Fi you use) and providers (your email, phone, internet and cloud storage companies).
    2. Go through the checklist (7 minutes). For each line write Yes, Partly, No or Not applicable. Menus differ between devices. If you cannot find a setting in a couple of minutes, write “unsure” and move on.
    3. Choose one change (3 minutes). Look at your No and Partly answers. Pick one that is small enough to do this week. Write it as a specific action with a when, for example “Turn on automatic updates on my laptop tonight”.
    4. Compare (2 minutes). Open the worked answer and compare how it picks a change.

    Devices

    1. Every device I use has a screen lock (passcode, fingerprint or face).
    2. My devices install updates, and none of them is so old that it no longer receives updates from its maker.
    3. If my phone or laptop were lost, I could find it or erase it remotely, and I have turned that feature on.
    4. I have a recent copy of the files and photos I could not replace, stored somewhere that is not always connected to the device.
    5. Before I sell, give away or recycle a device, I know how to reset it and sign out of my accounts.

    Apps and accounts

    1. I have used each app and account in the past year, or I have closed it.
    2. My email account, which can reset my other accounts, has two-step verification turned on.
    3. My banking and any cloud storage have two-step verification turned on.
    4. I install apps only from the official store for my device, and I have checked the permissions the apps ask for.
    5. I know which accounts have my payment card saved.

    Password storage
