    1. My passwords are kept in a password manager or another protected place, and not in a plain note or a notes app.
    2. Each important account has its own password.
    3. I know what I would do if I thought a password had been stolen.

    Networks

    1. My home Wi-Fi uses a password that I set, and not the one printed on the router.
    2. My router’s own settings are protected by a password that I set (if you have never looked, write “unsure”).
    3. When I use public Wi-Fi, I avoid banking and other sensitive tasks, or I use mobile data instead.
    4. Guests at home use a guest network or a separate password, if my router offers one.

    Providers

    1. I know which company holds my email, my photos and my backups.
    2. I have looked at what at least one of these providers says it does with my information, and what it lets me control.
    3. I know how to contact each provider, or report a problem, if my account is hacked.

    Your results are private, so there is no “right” set of answers. This worked answer shows what a good result and a good change look like. It is a fictional learner’s check, and part of the list only. Yours will be different.

    # Result Note
    1 Yes Phone and laptop are locked. The old tablet in the drawer has no passcode.
    2 Partly Laptop and phone update automatically. The old tablet has not been updated for years.
    4 No Photos are on the phone only.
    5 Unsure Has never reset a device.
    6 No Found about a dozen old accounts, including a forum from school.
    7 Yes Email has two-step verification.
    11 Partly Most passwords are in a password manager, and a few are in a phone note.
    14 Yes Changed the router password when it was installed.
    19 No Has never read what the cloud photo service does with photos.

    What a good change looks like. The learner has several gaps. They did not try to fix everything. They picked the gap that protects the most important thing and is small enough to do:

    My change: tonight I will move the passwords in my phone note into my password manager and delete the note.

    Why this is a good choice. It is specific (which passwords, and where they go). It has a when. It takes well under an hour. And it deals with a gap that could cause real harm. Other good changes from this list would be to turn on backups for the photos (item 4) or to close the old forum account (item 6). Any change is fine if it is real, specific and can be done this week.

    Not so good changes. “Be more careful online” is not specific. “Change all my passwords” is too big, and has no plan. “Buy an antivirus program” is a product, not a habit, and it does not deal with the gaps found.

    Checking yourself. You checked your own things only. You answered each line, or wrote “unsure”. Your change is one action with a when, and it contains no password or number. If you found nothing to change, pick a line you wrote “unsure” for and find out.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Sharing the checklist or a password. Keep your results to yourself. Never write a password, PIN or account number anywhere in this activity.
    • Choosing a change that is too big. “Fix everything” does not get done. Pick one action for this week.
    • Choosing a vague change. “Be safer” cannot be checked. Say what you will do and when.
    • Skipping the old things. The tablet in the drawer and the account from years ago are part of your ICT life too.
    • Feeling bad about the gaps. Almost everyone has some. The point is to make one change.
    • Checking other people’s devices or home network. This activity is only about your own.
    • Giving up because you could not find a setting. Write “unsure” and move on. Your device maker’s help pages show how.
    Challenge

    Challenge: Fix the awareness (10 minutes)

    A fictional scenario. A removalist firm emails a long security policy to everyone once a year. Months later, drivers still leave job sheets showing customers’ addresses on the seats of unlocked vans.

    Write a short plan to change what the drivers do. Use the five features from this episode: short, specific, role-based, repeated and safe to report. Your plan should say:

    1. who it is for and how long it takes,
    2. what example it uses,
    3. how often it is repeated,
    4. how a driver reports a slip, and
    5. how the firm will know that behaviour changed.

    Two to four lines for each point is enough. The scenario does not say who runs awareness at the firm, so name a role and say why you chose it.

    One worked answer. Yours may differ, and it can be sound with different details.

    1. Who and how long. Drivers, and anyone who rides with them. A 10-minute session at the start of a shift, not a document to read alone.
    2. Example. The firm’s own job sheet, held up in the session. Show what a stranger could learn from a sheet left on a seat: a name and an address. Then show the safe habit: keep sheets in a folder, take them with you, and lock the van.
    3. Repetition. In a new driver’s first week, then a 5-minute reminder at the depot every three months. Casual and part-time drivers get the same session.
    4. Reporting. A simple way to say “I left a sheet in the van”, for example a text to the depot supervisor. The firm says clearly that a reported slip is not punished, so drivers do not hide it.
    5. Checking. Not the number who attended. Instead, spot checks of parked vans for sheets in view, before and after, and the number of slips reported. If reports go up at first, that can be a good sign.

    Owner. The depot supervisor, because they see the drivers daily and can run a short session and do spot checks. The scenario does not say who this is at the firm, so this is a choice, and you could choose another role.

    Why the email did not work. It was long, general, sent to everyone, sent once a year, and gave no way to report. It fails all five features.

    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. A veterinary practice runs a 15-minute session on spotting fake supplier emails. Three months later, the manager wants evidence that staff behaviour has changed. Which measure is best?

      • A. The number of staff who attended the session, taken from the sign-in sheet.
      • B. How highly staff rated the session on the feedback form handed out straight afterwards.
      • C. Whether staff report more suspicious emails, and fewer click on risky ones.
      • D. Scores on a quiz that staff took on the day of the session, while it was fresh.

    2. Last year a firm named, in front of the whole team, the staff who clicked on a test phishing email. Now Lena has clicked on a real suspicious link. She is worried and thinks she should say nothing and hope it is fine. What would make her most likely to report it?

      • A. A reminder that the policy says all incidents must be reported.
      • B. A warning that anyone who hides a mistake will be disciplined.
      • C. A promise that reports are handled privately and without blame, and a simple way to make one.
      • D. A longer session on how phishing works.
    1. C. Reports and risky clicks are behaviour. More reports can be a good sign, because it means staff feel safe to speak up. Option A shows only that people were in the room. Option B shows that people enjoyed the session, not that their habits changed. Option D shows what people remember on the day, not what they do weeks later.
    2. C. People hide mistakes when they fear blame, and naming staff in public teaches exactly that. A promise of private, no-blame handling and an easy way to report deals with the real barrier. Options A and B repeat the rule or add a threat, which makes hiding more likely. Option D builds knowledge, but Lena already knows she clicked. Her problem is fear, not knowledge.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Write 3 to 6 sentences. This reflection is private to you. If you do this in a group, you choose what, if anything, to share with a partner. Describe your habits in general terms. Do not share passwords, answers to security questions, card numbers, account details or your address.

    • Your own ICT life. How secure is your personal ICT life? Think about the devices, social media, apps, password storage, network connections and service providers you use. Where are they, and how secure do you think each one is? Which one worries you most, and what was the one change you chose in the first challenge?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: personal ICT check 15, fix the awareness 10, quick check 5, discussion 5.

    Keep the personal check private. Do not ask anyone to read out, show or hand in their checklist, and do not walk around looking at screens. Remind the room that the worked answer is a fictional learner and guidance, not a set of correct personal answers. If you ask for anything at the end, ask only “who has picked a change?” and let people say as much or as little as they like. Remind everyone not to check anyone else’s devices or the venue’s network or router.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think awareness means a policy or a signed form. Ask what a driver or a receptionist did differently on Tuesday.
    • Learners measure attendance or satisfaction. Ask “what would you see if it worked?”
    • Learners choose an enormous change in the personal check. Ask “can you do that tonight?”
    • Learners feel ashamed of their gaps. Say that almost everyone has some.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share (see the general notes), but keep the pair stage general: “what kind of gap did you find?” and not “what is your password habit?” If anyone would rather not talk, let them write only.

    Tip. For the fix-the-awareness challenge, ask pairs to swap plans and check them against the five features, ticking each one.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Protect yourself gives plain-language advice on securing your own devices and accounts.
    • National Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Device security guidance is written for organisations. It is a UK page, and the Australian Cyber Security Centre is the local equivalent.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 5 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • Awareness is what people do on a busy day, not a policy in a folder.
    • Awareness works when it is short, specific, role-based, repeated and safe to report.
    • Check behaviour, such as reports and spot checks, and not attendance. More reports can be a good sign.
    • Your own habits come to work with you, so check your own ICT life privately and choose one small, specific change with a when.
    • Awareness, vetting and access each have a limit, so a good plan uses all three.

    References

    Bartlett, J. (2018) The People Vs Tech: How the internet is killing democracy (and how we save it). London: Ebury Press.

    Australian Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Protect yourself. Available at: https://www.cyber.gov.au/protect-yourself (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    National Cyber Security Centre (n.d.) Device security guidance. Available at: https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/device-security-guidance (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Vetting, trust and access

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What can vetting tell an organisation about a person, and what can it not tell?
    • Why is vetting only one layer of protection?
    • How can compartmentalisation limit what any one person can reach or know, and what does it cost the people who work under it?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • explain what vetting can and cannot tell an organisation, including the idea of ongoing assessment (ULO 2)
    • explain why vetting is only one layer of protection (ULO 2)
    • use compartmentalisation to limit what any one person can reach or know, and weigh its cost to staff (ULO 2)

    This episode matches Week 5 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Security awareness that changes behaviour, which covered the first of three people-controls. This episode covers the other two: who is let in, and how much any one person can reach.

    What is vetting?

    Vetting means checking a person before you give them trust and access. An ordinary employer might confirm identity, check that qualifications are real, call referees and, for some roles, check criminal history. For roles that handle highly sensitive information, such as in government, the checks go deeper and are repeated.

    In Australia, the Australian Government’s Protective Security Policy Framework (PSPF) sets protective security expectations for government agencies. It includes personnel security, which is deciding who is suitable to be given access and keeping that decision under review (Protective Security Policy Framework, n.d.). The framework is written for government agencies, not for a small business. It is useful because it shows how a large organisation describes the idea that trust is checked before access is given, and then checked again. A link is in Go deeper below.

    What can vetting do? It lowers the chance of hiring someone who is not who they say they are, or who has a record that matters for the job. That is valuable. But it has limits.

    What vetting cannot do

    • It is a snapshot. A check shows what was true on the day it was done. People’s lives change. A person with a clean record can later be in financial trouble, become angry at their employer, or be pressured by someone else.
    • It only finds what has been recorded. A clean result means nothing has been recorded against the person. It does not mean they will behave well.
    • It cannot read intentions.
    • It can be uneven. Checks can be skipped for people who already seem trusted, and that is when they matter. Checks must also be fair. They should be proportionate to the access the role gives. Checking a gardener as hard as a finance officer is a waste, and may be unfair.

    Many organisations also ask staff to report changes that might matter for the role, such as a new outside job. They treat these reports fairly and privately. The idea is that trust is not given once and then forgotten. This is called ongoing assessment.

    This is why good organisations treat vetting as one layer. After the check they keep reviewing, they listen to staff, and they limit access.

    Compartmentalisation

    Think of the compartments in a ship: sealed sections, so that if one floods the whole ship does not sink. In security, compartmentalisation means limiting each person’s access to systems, and their knowledge, to what their job needs. You may remember least privilege from Identity, identity management and identity theft. Compartmentalisation is the wider idea. It covers who can open what, who knows what, and how systems are kept apart.

    There are three kinds.

    Kind Idea Example
    Access Each person can open only what their job needs. The accounts team can open the accounts folder, and not the staff records.
    Knowledge Each person knows only the part of the work they need. A café chain sends each branch a pre-mixed base for its signature sauce, so no single branch knows the whole recipe.
    Systems Systems are kept apart, so a problem in one does not spread freely to another. A business keeps its guest Wi-Fi on a different network from its customer files.

    Why it helps

    You cannot predict every mistake or every betrayal. Vetting is a snapshot, and awareness can fail on a bad day. Compartments limit the damage when something goes wrong. If one person’s account is taken over, or one person turns bad, they can reach only their own compartment, and not everything.

    What it costs

    Compartments have costs.

    • People may need to ask for access, and work may slow down.
    • A person who is the only one with access becomes a single point of failure when they are sick or on leave.

    So plan for it. Decide who can cover, and have a recorded, approved way to get extra access in an emergency. Review who has access at set times, because compartments weaken as people change jobs. A simple record helps: for each system or folder, who owns it, who may open it, and when that was last checked. If nobody can say who owns a folder, nobody is looking after who can open it.

    Why people need to understand it

    Compartments work best when people understand why they exist. If staff think access limits mean they are distrusted, they look for ways around them. If they know the limit protects them too, because a problem cannot be pinned on someone who could never have reached the data, they are more likely to accept it. This links to People at work: BYOD and working from home, where a rule’s burden pushed people towards shortcuts.

    A case to work on

    The next two challenges use a short fictional case, so that you can see the limits of vetting in practice. Use only the text below. Where it does not say something, write “the scenario does not say”, or use “could” or “may”.

    Larkspur Marine is a fictional engineering firm. It gives a new systems administrator full access to every server on his first day, because he has a clearance. Six months later, he copies a large part of the customer database to a personal device. The firm’s hiring check noticed an unexplained gap in his work history, and nobody followed it up.

    The scenario does not say what the clearance covered, what the gap was, whether anyone reviewed his access during the six months, how the copying was found, or why he did it. Do not guess. The questions are about controls, not about judging him.

    Challenge

    Challenge: What did the checks miss? (10 minutes)

    Read the case (2 minutes). Then answer in two to four sentences (8 minutes).

    What did the checks miss, or fail to catch? Name two points from the case, and say for each why a check could not have caught it, or why it may not have been followed up.

    Any two points that the case supports are accepted. Here are three.

    • A noticed gap that nobody followed up. The hiring check found an unexplained gap in his work history, and nobody followed it up. That is a check that found something and then stopped. The scenario does not say how large the gap was or what it hid, so a good answer does not claim that the gap explains what happened later. It only says that a flag was raised and not answered.
    • A clearance is a snapshot. He was given full access because he has a clearance. A clearance shows that someone was judged suitable at one point in time. It cannot show what he would decide six months later. The scenario does not say what the clearance covered.
    • No review after day one. The scenario does not say whether anyone reviewed his access or his behaviour in the six months. A good answer says the case is silent, and not that no review existed. It can still say that nothing in the case shows one, and that a review could have raised the alarm earlier.

    Checking yourself. You used the case only. You said “the scenario does not say” or “could” where it is silent. You gave two points, each with a reason.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Limit the reach (10 minutes)

    Use the same case. Answer in two to four sentences each. Use “could” or “may” for anything the case does not state.

    1. How might compartmentalisation have changed the outcome? Choose one kind (access, knowledge or systems), say what the limit would have been, and say how it could have reduced the amount one person could reach.
    2. What is the cost of that limit? A person in a systems role may need wide access to do the job. Name one cost or difficulty of limiting it, and one way to reduce the cost.
    3. Which one people-control would you recommend? It can be an awareness activity, a rule or an access limit. Say who would own it. The owner should be a role, not “all staff” or “management”.

    1. Compartmentalisation (one kind is enough).

    • Access. He had full access to every server on his first day. If his role had given him only the servers his tasks needed, the customer database may not have been among them, or a smaller part of it could have been reachable. The scenario does not say what his tasks were, so a good answer says “could”.
    • Systems. If the customer database had sat in a separate system that needed separate approval, a general administrator account would not have opened it. The scenario does not say how the firm’s systems were arranged.
    • Knowledge. This fits the case less well, because the case is about what he could reach, and not about what he knew. A good answer can say so.

    Do not say that compartmentalisation would have prevented the copying. The case does not show that. Say it could have reduced how much he could reach.

    2. The cost. A systems administrator may need to reach many servers to fix problems. If access is split too tightly, urgent fixes slow down, and people may look for shortcuts. That is the burden from People at work. Ways to reduce the cost: split the administrator job into separate roles, give extra access only for a task and take it away afterwards, record when extra access is used, or use a two-person rule for the most sensitive actions (you met this in The insider threat).

    3. One people-control (examples).

    • Rule. Access to the customer database needs a second person’s approval, and the database’s owner reviews use each month. Owner: the head of IT security.
    • Review. Check the access and work history of anyone in a trusted role at set times, and not only at hiring, and follow up every flag raised in a hiring check. Owner: the HR manager for the follow-up, and the head of IT security for the access review.
    • Rule. New starters get the access their role needs on day one, and more only when their manager asks for it. Owner: the IT service manager.

    Checking yourself. In question 1 you named a kind of limit and said how it could reduce the reach, without claiming it would have stopped everything. In question 2 you gave a cost and a fix. In question 3 you named a control and an owner.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Guessing why he did it. The scenario gives no reason. The task is about controls, not about his motives.
    • Stating what the scenario does not say as fact. It does not say what the gap was, what the clearance covered, or whether anyone reviewed his access. Use “the scenario does not say”, “could” or “may”.
    • Saying “vetting failed completely”. The check noticed the gap. The failure was that nobody followed it up, and that a clearance alone was treated as enough.
    • Saying compartmentalisation would have prevented it. It may have limited how much he could reach.
    • Forgetting the cost. Limits slow people down. A good plan says how to reduce the burden.
    • Adding facts from outside the case. Use the text only, so that your answers can be checked.
    • Suggesting a control with no owner. Every control needs a person or role responsible.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. A firm checks a new warehouse manager’s identity, licence and referees, and everything is clean. On his first day, it gives him access to every system, because he has been checked. What is the main problem?

      • A. Vetting is one layer among several, so his access should still match what the job needs.
      • B. The check should also have included his school results, his hobbies and his social media accounts outside work.
      • C. A clean check means the firm can rely on him, so full access is reasonable.
      • D. Warehouse managers should be given access in stages over their first year.

    2. A company asks staff who approve supplier payments to tell HR if a close relative starts working for a supplier. It promises to treat each report privately and fairly. What is the main purpose?

      • A. To build a file that lets the company dismiss staff more quickly.
      • B. To keep trust under review after hiring, so a risk from a change can be discussed early.
      • C. To replace the checks that were made when the staff were first hired.
      • D. To make sure staff keep an eye on each other and report any odd behaviour.

    3. A game studio is making a game it has not announced. It briefs each contractor only on the level they are building, and not on the whole story. What benefit does this give the studio most directly?

      • A. Contractors can be approved more quickly, with less paperwork for each one.
      • B. The studio can stop checking who its contractors are, since each one knows so little.
      • C. The game will be of better quality overall, because each person can focus on one part.
      • D. If one contractor leaks or loses their files, only part of the game is exposed.
    1. A. A clean check shows the past, not what he will decide later, so access should still be limited to what the job needs. Option B would be an unfair and disproportionate check. Option C treats vetting as the only layer. Option D is not the main problem, because the issue is that access does not match the job at all.
    2. B. This is ongoing assessment: trust is not checked once and forgotten. It works only if staff believe they will be treated fairly. Option A is wrong because reports handled privately and fairly are meant to support staff and the company, not to prepare dismissals. Option C is wrong because reports add to the first checks and do not replace them. Option D is wrong because the reports are about a person’s own changes, not about watching colleagues.
    3. D. Compartmentalising knowledge means that no single person holds the whole picture, so one leak or loss does limited harm. Option A is wrong because briefing contractors separately does not speed up approval. Option B is wrong because limits on knowledge are one layer, and they do not replace checks. Option C is wrong because quality is not what limits on knowledge are for.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one or both prompts and write 3 to 6 sentences for each. Do not name private individuals or share private details such as passwords.

    • When checks fail. You worked on one case. What real cases do you know of, or have you heard of, in which an organisation’s checks on a person did not prevent harm, and what did they lead to? (If you cannot name one, think about what you would want an organisation to change after such a case.) Which kind of change do you think matters most: better checks on people, limits on what each person can reach, or better awareness for everyone? Why?
    • Vetting and its limits. Australia has vetting requirements, for example for people who handle sensitive government information. Why do you think problems still happen, even where checks are strict? What does that tell you about how an organisation should treat its own staff, in both trust and in limits?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 25 minutes. Exercises 30 minutes: what did the checks miss 10, limit the reach 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. The Larkspur Marine case is short and is read inside the first challenge.

    Handling the case. The case, Larkspur Marine, is fictional. Keep learners to the text: where it is silent, they say “the scenario does not say” or use “could” or “may”. If learners bring up real cases they know of, keep the focus on controls (“what could have limited the reach of one person?”) rather than on whether the person was right, and treat details offered from memory as unverified.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners say vetting “failed completely” or that it is useless. The point is that a check is a snapshot and one layer.
    • Learners add facts the case does not give. Ask them to use “could” or “may”, or to say the scenario does not say.
    • Learners say compartmentalisation would have prevented the whole event. Ask what it could have reduced.
    • Learners forget the cost to staff, or suggest a control with no owner.
    • Learners think strict checks mean no risk. This links to the second discussion prompt.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share (see the general notes). Ask a pair that disagrees about which change matters most to explain their reasons. The strongest answers say that the three changes work together.

    Tip. Ask pairs to draw a one-line ship on the board and mark which compartment their chosen control would seal.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Protective Security Policy Framework (n.d.) Personnel security is the Australian Government’s guidance on personnel security. It is written for government agencies, so use it to see how a large organisation thinks about checking trust before access and again afterwards.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 5 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • Vetting checks a person before you give them trust and access. It lowers risk, and it is valuable.
    • A check is a snapshot. It finds only what was recorded, and it cannot read intentions, so vetting is one layer and not the whole answer.
    • Ongoing assessment keeps trust under review after hiring, and it works only when staff are treated fairly and privately.
    • Compartmentalisation limits access, knowledge and systems to what each job needs, so one mistake or one bad decision does limited harm.
    • Limits have costs for staff, so plan cover and emergency access, review who has access, explain why, and give every control an owner.

    References

    Protective Security Policy Framework (n.d.) Personnel security. Available at: https://www.protectivesecurity.gov.au/personnel-security (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Australian privacy law and data breaches

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Who does the Privacy Act cover, and which Australian Privacy Principle fits a given privacy problem?
    • What must an organisation do when it suspects a data breach?
    • What did the 2024 changes and the Cyber Security Act 2024 add?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • explain who the Privacy Act covers, and why a council-run body may be covered by a different law (ULO 3)
    • match a situation to the Australian Privacy Principle (APP) it most clearly affects (ULO 3)
    • explain what the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme asks of an organisation, and what the 2024 changes and the Cyber Security Act 2024 added (ULO 3)

    This episode matches Week 6 of The Human Firewall microcredential. The second half of the week is in the next episode, Responding to identity theft, and what comes next. It builds on Privacy and privacy impact assessments, which asked what a privacy risk is. This one asks what the law says about it.

    This is general information for learning, not legal advice. The law changes, so check the official pages linked under Go deeper before you rely on any detail.

    The Privacy Act and the APPs

    The main privacy law is the Privacy Act 1988. It is a Commonwealth law. Its purpose is to protect the privacy of individuals and to set rules for how personal information is handled.

    The heart of the Act is 13 Australian Privacy Principles, or APPs. The OAIC (n.d.a) says they apply to some private sector organisations and to most Australian Government agencies. Together these are called APP entities.

    Which private organisations are covered?

    • Generally, those with an annual turnover of more than three million dollars.
    • Many small businesses are outside the Act.
    • One important exception is this. A private health service provider that holds health information is covered even if it is small (OAIC n.d.e). That includes GPs, dentists, pharmacists and allied health professionals. A small clinic cannot say it is too small to matter.

    Health information is a kind of sensitive information. The law asks for extra care with sensitive information, because the harm from its exposure can be much greater.

    Which law covers a council-run library?

    Riverbend Community Library is run by a local council. A local council is not a Commonwealth agency, and it is generally covered by the privacy law of its state or territory rather than by the Privacy Act. Those state and territory laws have their own principles. They ask many of the same questions as the APPs, but the wording, the coverage and the rules about reporting breaches differ from place to place. The Riverbend page does not say which state the library is in.

    So this episode does not claim that the APPs legally bind Riverbend. In the challenges you will treat Riverbend as if it were covered by the APPs. That is a teaching device. The APPs are the national set of principles, and the questions they ask (what do you collect, what do you tell people, how do you use it, how do you keep it safe, what do people get back) are questions any privacy law asks. In real life, the first step is to find out which law applies to the organisation in front of you.

    Sorting the APPs by stage

    You do not need to memorise thirteen numbers. Ask instead: at what stage of the information’s life did the problem happen?

    • Collecting: what did the organisation ask for, and did it explain why?
    • Using and sharing: did it use or pass on information for a purpose it should not have?
    • Keeping safe: did it protect the information, and delete it when it was no longer needed?
    • Open and fair: can people find out how the organisation handles information, see what it holds and ask for corrections?

    The nine APPs used in the challenges are below. These are plain-language summaries, based on the OAIC’s quick reference (OAIC n.d.a). The OAIC page lists all 13. The ones not shown are APP 2 (anonymity and pseudonymity), APP 4 (unsolicited information), APP 9 (government related identifiers) and APP 10 (quality of information).

    APP Name What it asks, in plain words
    APP 1 Open and transparent management of personal information Have a clear, up-to-date privacy policy, make it available, and have practices and systems to follow the APPs and handle privacy questions and complaints
    APP 3 Collection of solicited personal information Collect only what is reasonably necessary for what the organisation does, with higher standards for sensitive information
    APP 5 Notification of the collection of personal information When you collect information, take reasonable steps to tell people who you are, why you are collecting it and who it usually goes to
    APP 6 Use or disclosure of personal information Use or share information only for the purpose it was collected, unless an exception applies (for example, the person agrees)
    APP 7 Direct marketing Marketing uses of personal information have their own conditions, including an easy way to opt out and acting on opt-out requests. The marketing rules sit in APP 7, not APP 6
    APP 8 Cross-border disclosure of personal information Before information goes overseas, take reasonable steps to make sure the overseas recipient will protect it
    APP 11 Security of personal information Take reasonable steps to protect information from misuse, interference, loss and unauthorised access or disclosure, and to destroy or de-identify it when it is no longer needed
    APP 12 Access to personal information Give people access to the information you hold about them when they ask, unless a specific exception applies. If you refuse, give written reasons
    APP 13 Correction of personal information Take reasonable steps to correct information when it is wrong or when the person asks. If you refuse, give written reasons and the ways to complain

    Here is a trap to watch for. If an outsider gets in because protection was weak, think APP 11. If the organisation itself chooses to use or pass on information for a new purpose, think APP 6, or APP 7 if the new purpose is marketing.

    Two more things are worth knowing. APP 8 means the organisation stays accountable if an overseas recipient does not protect the information. And since December 2024, the law says the reasonable steps in APP 11 include technical measures (such as locks and encryption) and organisational measures (such as policies, procedures and staff training).

    When things go wrong: data breaches

    A data breach is when personal information is lost, or accessed or disclosed without authorisation. The OAIC gives examples such as a lost or stolen device, a hacked database and information sent to the wrong person (OAIC n.d.c).

    Under the Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) scheme, an organisation or agency covered by the Privacy Act must tell the people affected, and the OAIC, about a breach that is likely to cause serious harm. “Likely” means more probable than not. Serious harm can include identity theft, financial loss through fraud, a risk of physical harm, serious psychological harm, or serious damage to a person’s reputation. Health details, or several details together, such as a name, birth date and address, make serious harm more likely.

    As with the APPs, the scheme is written for APP entities. A council body may be under a different state or territory arrangement for breach notification, so in the challenges you again treat Riverbend as if it were covered.

    There are three steps.

    1. Assess. An organisation that suspects a breach must assess quickly whether serious harm is likely. The OAIC says generally an organisation has 30 days to assess, but quicker is better, because harm can grow while it waits.
    2. Act. If the organisation quickly fixes the problem so that serious harm is no longer likely, it does not need to notify.
    3. Tell. If serious harm is likely, the organisation tells the individuals and the OAIC. The notice includes the organisation’s name and contact details, a description of the breach, the kinds of information involved, and the steps people should take.

    Two more points. If an organisation has sent information overseas under the usual rule and the overseas recipient has a breach, the Australian organisation is still responsible for assessing it and notifying. And when two organisations hold the information, the OAIC suggests that the one with the most direct relationship with the people affected may be best placed to tell them.

    This is why a hidden mistake is so costly. If staff are afraid to report a breach, the organisation loses the time it needs to assess and act. That is a legal reason for a no-blame reporting rule, and not only a kindness.

    What changed recently

    Parliament passed the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2024 in late November 2024; it became law in December 2024. The changes most relevant to you are these.

    • A statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy. A tort is a civil wrong that a person can sue over. It began on 10 June 2025. The OAIC lists two kinds: intruding upon someone’s seclusion, and misusing information about them (OAIC 2025). A person can sue another person or an organisation in court. It is not limited to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, and the OAIC does not run these cases.
    • Stronger enforcement. New tiers of civil penalties, and infringement notices.
    • APP 11 wording. The technical and organisational measures described above.
    • An overseas list. A way to prescribe countries and schemes with adequate privacy protection.
    • Automated decisions. From 10 December 2026, privacy policies must describe the kinds of personal information and decisions involved in certain automated decisions.

    For a health clinic, for example, the tort means a person who snoops in records could face a claim as well as the clinic, and the regulator has more ways to act short of going to court.

    There is a second law. The Cyber Security Act 2024 includes minimum standards for smart devices, a Cyber Incident Review Board, and mandatory ransomware payment reporting. Ransomware is malicious software that locks data so criminals can demand money. Under the reporting rule, a business that carries on business in Australia, with annual turnover of more than three million dollars, must report a ransomware or cyber extortion payment that it made, or knows was made for it, within 72 hours, using a form on ReportCyber (Australian Signals Directorate n.d.). Responsible entities for critical infrastructure assets must also report a ransomware payment, whatever their turnover. The rules started on 30 May 2025. The law asks for a report after a payment is made. It does not tell anyone whether to pay.

    Try it on Riverbend

    The challenges use Riverbend Community Library, a made-up library. Read that page once before you start. It describes how the library works. It does not tell you what is right or wrong with it. Each scenario below is a separate, made-up event. None of them says what Riverbend actually does.

    Challenge

    Challenge: Match ten Riverbend events to the APP (15 minutes)

    The situation. Treat Riverbend as if it were covered by the APPs, as explained above. For each event, work only from what the event says.

    1. A volunteer saves a spreadsheet copy of the member list in an online folder that is set so anyone with the link can open it. A member’s neighbour finds the link in a web search and can read members’ names, addresses and dates of birth.
    2. Riverbend puts the children’s session sign-up on an online form. It asks for each child’s name, age and allergies and the carer’s phone number. The form does not say who runs the sessions, why the details are needed or who may receive them.
    3. Members’ email addresses were collected to send overdue notices. The library manager now uses them to email promotions for a local business that has paid for the space. Members who reply “STOP” or click “unsubscribe” keep getting the emails.
    4. A member asks in writing for a copy of the information the library holds about her. A desk volunteer says, “We don’t give those out,” and nothing is put in writing. Nothing in the event suggests that handing over the information would put anyone at risk.
    5. The new-member form asks every applicant for their employer’s name, their past home addresses and a copy of their passport. To issue a library card, the library needs a name, an address and a way to contact the member.
    6. The library manager signs up with an online storage company to keep a copy of the member database. The company’s servers are in another country. The contract has no privacy terms, and nobody has looked into how the company protects the data.
    7. A caller who says he is a member’s employer phones the front desk. A volunteer reads out the member’s borrowing history, which includes books about challenging a dismissal. The member has not agreed to this.
    8. In a cupboard, Riverbend still has paper sign-up sheets for children’s sessions from more than ten years ago. They list children’s names and allergies. There is no reason to keep them and no process for destroying them.
    9. A member emails to ask for a copy of the library’s privacy policy. There is no privacy policy to send, nobody knows who deals with privacy questions, and the email is never answered.
    10. A carer tells the library twice, once in writing, that her phone number in the children’s program record is wrong and asks for it to be corrected. Months later the record still shows the old number, and she has had no reply.

    Use the nine APPs in the table above.

    1. Read the table (3 minutes).
    2. Sort the ten events (12 minutes). For each event, write the APP number it most clearly affects and one line saying why. Use only the facts in the event. Each event has one best fit, and two events share an APP.

    One worked answer. Your wording will differ. A reason is sound if it points to a fact in the event.

    # APP One-line reason
    1 APP 11 The folder was open to anyone with the link, so an outsider could read the information. This is about keeping information safe
    2 APP 5 The form collects personal information but does not say who is collecting it, why, or who may receive it
    3 APP 7 The use is direct marketing, and requests to opt out are ignored. Marketing has its own principle
    4 APP 12 The member asked for access to the information held about her and was refused with no reason in writing. The event shows no exception
    5 APP 3 The form asks for more than is reasonably necessary to issue a library card
    6 APP 8 The data goes overseas, and nobody has taken reasonable steps to check that the company will protect it
    7 APP 6 Borrowing information collected to lend books was passed to a caller for a different purpose, and the member has not agreed
    8 APP 11 Information that is no longer needed is still held, and there is no process to destroy or de-identify it
    9 APP 1 There is no privacy policy to provide, and no person or process to deal with privacy questions
    10 APP 13 The carer asked for a correction, and the library neither corrected the record nor replied

    Alternatives and why. Where two answers fit, a clear reason is accepted. Event 3 is the exception.

    • Event 3: APP 6 is not accepted. The OAIC’s APP 6 guidelines say APP 6 does not apply to use or disclosure for direct marketing, because APP 7 covers it (OAIC n.d.d).
    • Event 10: APP 10 (quality of personal information) is about keeping information accurate when it is collected, used or disclosed. It is a reasonable second thought, but the carer asked for a correction, which is the heart of APP 13.
    • Event 6: APP 11 could be argued, because the data needs protecting. APP 8 is the closer fit because the key fact is that the data goes overseas with no checks.

    If you got four or more wrong, ask: at what stage of the information’s life did the problem happen: collecting, using or sharing, keeping safe, or giving back to the person?

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Using APP 11 for every problem. APP 11 is about keeping information safe and deleting it when it is not needed. If the organisation itself chooses to pass information on for another purpose, that is usually APP 6.
    • Using APP 6 for marketing. In event 3 the use is plain direct marketing, and the opt-out requests are ignored, so APP 7 is the best fit. Look for the opt-out.
    • Mixing up APP 5 and APP 1. APP 5 is the notice you give at the time you collect. APP 1 is the privacy policy and the systems behind it.
    • Mixing up APP 3 and APP 5. APP 3 is about what you collect. APP 5 is about telling people that you are collecting it.
    • Adding facts the event does not give. If it does not say what the library did next, do not assume. Use “could” in your reasons where you are guessing.
    • Forgetting that two answers can be the same APP. Do not change a correct answer only because you used it already.
    • Writing only the number. The task asks for the number and a reason. The reason is what shows you understand.
    Challenge

    Challenge: Is it a data breach? (10 minutes)

    Use events 1 and 7 from the previous challenge, and keep treating Riverbend as if it were covered.

    1. Event 1 (3 minutes). In one or two sentences, say whether it could be a data breach, and what Riverbend would need to assess next.
    2. Event 7 (3 minutes). Do the same.
    3. The law behind it (4 minutes). Riverbend is run by a council. In two or three sentences, say why this lesson treats it “as if” the APPs and the NDB scheme applied, and what you would check in real life.

    One worked answer.

    1. Event 1. It could be a data breach, because information has been accessed without authorisation. Riverbend would need to assess quickly whether serious harm is likely. The files hold names, addresses and dates of birth, and several details together make serious harm more likely. It would also look at who could have seen them. The event does not say how many members are in the file, or whether anyone but the neighbour opened it. Riverbend would also ask whether it can fix the problem fast, for example by closing the link, so that harm is no longer likely.
    2. Event 7. It could be a data breach, because information has been disclosed without authorisation. Riverbend would need to assess whether serious harm is likely. That means thinking about what the borrowing history could mean for this member, given that it includes books about challenging a dismissal, and what the caller might do with it. The event does not say whether the caller really is the member’s employer.
    3. The law behind it. A council is not a Commonwealth agency, and local councils are generally covered by state or territory privacy law rather than the Privacy Act. The APPs are the national set of principles, so they are a sensible benchmark for practice. In real life I would check which state or territory law applies to the library, what it says about reporting breaches, and who handles privacy questions at the council. The Riverbend page names no one for this, so I would not assume who is responsible until I had checked.

    An organisation assesses a suspected breach to decide whether it must notify. Assessing is a separate step from deciding which APP was affected.

    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Saying every breach must be notified. Only a breach that is likely to cause serious harm, and that is not fixed in time, must be notified. The assessment decides.
    • Waiting for 30 days. Thirty days is generally the limit for finishing the assessment, not a period in which nothing needs to happen.
    • Waiting until you are certain. “Likely” means more probable than not. Organisations assess a suspected breach.
    • Stating that the APPs bind Riverbend. A council is generally covered by state or territory law. Say “as if” and name what you would check.
    • Guessing facts the event does not give. Say “the event does not say”.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. On 3 March, the owner of a bookshop chain covered by the Privacy Act suspects that someone else has been using a staff member’s email account, which holds customer details. She says, “The rules give me 30 days, so I will look into it in April.” What is the best advice?

      • A. She is right, because the scheme gives 30 days before the assessment even needs to start.
      • B. She should wait until she is certain that someone has used the customer details.
      • C. She should notify the customers at once and skip the assessment, to be on the safe side.
      • D. She should assess promptly, because 30 days is generally the limit, and harm may grow.

    2. A two-person speech pathology practice has an annual turnover well under three million dollars. The owner says the Privacy Act does not apply, because the practice is a small business. Is the owner right?

      • A. Yes, because only businesses with a turnover over three million dollars are covered.
      • B. No, because a private health service provider that holds health information is covered even if it is small.
      • C. Yes, because the Act covers only hospitals and not private practices.
      • D. No, but only if the practice has more than one staff member.

    3. An Australian furniture maker with annual turnover of twelve million dollars pays a ransom to get its files back. What must it do?

      • A. Report the payment within 72 hours using the ransomware payment form.
      • B. Report only if the files were not returned.
      • C. Report within 72 hours of receiving the demand, even if it did not pay.
      • D. Nothing, because only critical infrastructure must report.
    1. D. Thirty days is generally the limit for assessing, and harm can grow while an organisation waits, so quicker is better. Option A treats the 30 days as a waiting period, and option B waits for certainty when the test is “likely”. Option C skips the assessment, which is the step that decides whether notifying is needed.
    2. B. A private health service provider that holds health information is covered by the Privacy Act, whatever its size. Option A forgets this exception, option C is wrong about who is covered, and option D invents a staffing test.
    3. A. The rule applies after a payment is made by a business over the turnover threshold. The report is about the payment, so option C is wrong, and option B adds a condition that is not in the rule. Option D is wrong because the rule is not limited to critical infrastructure.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one prompt and write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords, card numbers or account details.

    • Protecting yourself with encryption. Can you use encryption to protect yourself? Think about what you do already (for example a screen lock, a messaging app or a secure website) and what encryption cannot do. What is one thing you could start doing, or stop doing, to protect your own information?
    • Owning up quickly. The breach scheme works best when mistakes are reported fast. What would make you report a mistake at work, such as a message sent to the wrong person, within the hour? What would stop you?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: match ten events 15, is it a data breach 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 3 minutes at the start of the first challenge.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners think small organisations are never covered. Use the health service provider exception.
    • Learners use APP 11 for everything, or APP 6 for marketing. Ask “what stage of the information’s life?” and “is there an opt-out?”.
    • Learners think every breach must be notified, or that 30 days is a waiting period.
    • Learners say the APPs apply to Riverbend because they apply to “privacy”. Ask who runs Riverbend, and what that means for which law applies.
    • Learners add facts to the events. Ask them to say “the event does not say”.

    Running the discussion. The first prompt is personal, so ask pairs to share one habit they could change, not their own settings. For the second, ask what the organisation could do so that reporting feels safe.

    Tip. If you are teaching in a particular state or territory, spend two minutes finding its privacy law for councils and say so aloud. It shows learners that “which law applies” is a real question with a checkable answer. Remind them that this is general information and not legal advice.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.b) The Privacy Act says what the Act is for and who it covers.
    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.a) Australian Privacy Principles quick reference lists all 13 principles.
    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.c) What is a notifiable data breach? explains serious harm and the notice.
    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.e) What is a health service provider? explains why small health services are covered.
    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (2025) Statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy describes the new right to sue.
    • Australian Signals Directorate (n.d.) Ransomware payment and cyber extortion payment reporting says who must report and the 72-hour limit.
    • The Cyber Security Act 2024 and the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 are on the Federal Register of Legislation. They are written for lawyers.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 6 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • The Privacy Act and its 13 APPs bind most Australian Government agencies and some private organisations. Many small businesses are outside it, but a private health service provider that holds health information is covered whatever its size.
    • A council-run body is generally covered by state or territory privacy law instead. Find out which law applies before you say what an organisation must do.
    • To pick the APP, ask what stage of the information’s life the problem happened at. Outsiders getting in is usually APP 11. The organisation choosing a new use is usually APP 6, or APP 7 for marketing.
    • For a suspected breach: assess quickly, act to reduce harm, and tell the people affected and the OAIC if serious harm is likely.
    • The 2024 changes added a right to sue for serious invasions of privacy, stronger enforcement and APP 11 wording on technical and organisational measures. The Cyber Security Act 2024 requires some businesses to report ransomware payments within 72 hours.

    References

    Australian Signals Directorate (n.d.) Ransomware payment and cyber extortion payment reporting. Available at: https://www.cyber.gov.au/report-and-recover/report/ransomware-payment-and-cyber-extortion-payment-reporting (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Cyber Security Act 2024 (Cth). Available at: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2024A00098/asmade/text (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) (n.d.a) Australian Privacy Principles quick reference. Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-quick-reference (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    OAIC (n.d.b) The Privacy Act. Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/the-privacy-act (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    OAIC (n.d.c) What is a notifiable data breach? Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/your-privacy-rights/data-breaches/what-is-a-notifiable-data-breach (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    OAIC (n.d.d) Chapter 6: APP 6 Use or disclosure of personal information. Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-6-app-6-use-or-disclosure-of-personal-information (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    OAIC (n.d.e) What is a health service provider? Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/your-privacy-rights/health-information/what-is-a-health-service-provider (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    OAIC (2025) Statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy [web page], 19 June. Available at: https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/your-privacy-rights/more-privacy-rights/statutory-tort-for-serious-invasions-of-privacy (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (Cth). Available at: https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2024A00128/asmade/text (Accessed: 2 November 2026).

    Content from Responding to identity theft, and what comes next

    Last updated on 2026-11-02 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 55 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • In what order should a person respond when their identity is stolen, and why does the order matter?
    • How might cybercrime, cyber war, connected devices, big data and quantum computing change people’s lives?
    • Who is in charge of the internet, and what can you do about your own part of it?

    Objectives

    By the end of this episode you can:

    • put the steps for responding to identity theft in a sensible order, and say why each one matters (ULO 2)
    • decide which steps a particular case adds, moves or leaves out (ULO 2)
    • describe, in a sentence each, how cybercrime, cyber war, connected devices, big data and quantum computing may change people’s lives (ULO 2)
    • say who has a say over what happens online: governments, platform companies and your own choices (ULO 2)

    This episode matches Week 6 of The Human Firewall microcredential. It follows Australian privacy law and data breaches, which looked at what the law asks of organisations. This one looks at what a person can do when something goes wrong for them, and then at the wider world beyond the library, the clinic and the office.

    This is general information for learning, not legal advice or personal advice.

    Responding to identity theft

    You met identity theft in Identity, identity management and identity theft: someone uses your personal details to pretend to be you. This episode is about what to do next.

    The order of the first steps matters. Some steps stop money leaving. Others repair the damage over weeks. A good order does the urgent things first, then the repair, then the long wait.

    1. Stop the money. Contact your bank or card provider, using the number on your card or in the official app.
    2. Secure your accounts. Change passwords from a device you trust, use a strong, unique password for each account, and turn on multi-factor authentication.
    3. Get support. IDCARE is Australia and New Zealand’s national identity and cyber support service. A case manager can help you make a plan for your situation (IDCARE n.d.).
    4. Check your credit. A stolen licence or Medicare card could be used to apply for credit. You can ask a credit reporting body for a free credit report, dispute anything you do not recognise and consider a credit ban.
    5. Make a report. The Australian Signals Directorate (2026) points people to ReportCyber on cyber.gov.au. If it was an online scam, report it to Scamwatch too. If your tax file number is involved, contact the Australian Taxation Office.
    6. Replace stolen documents. Follow your state or territory’s advice. For a passport, tell the Australian Passport Office. A Medicare card is replaced through Services Australia.
    7. Complain, if an organisation mishandled your information. The OAIC asks you to complain to the organisation first. If it does not respond in a reasonable time (generally 30 days) or does not resolve it, you may be able to complain to the OAIC (OAIC n.d.). Only some organisations are covered by the Privacy Act, as you saw in the last episode. If the organisation is a council-run body, a state or territory regulator may be the right place instead, so check which applies.
    8. Keep checking. Watch your accounts, mail and messages. Criminals may not use stolen details straight away.

    A report does not stop money leaving, so it comes after the urgent steps. Two habits protect you at every step. Use the number on your card, the official app, or a website you type in yourself, and never a number or link from a message or caller. And do not assume an organisation was at fault unless you have a reason to think so.

    If your own identity has been stolen, do not wait to finish this episode. Start with your bank, and visit IDCARE and ReportCyber directly by typing the address yourself.

    Cybercrime, cyber war and the future

    The rest of this episode is a light look at the wider world. It is here to start your thinking, and you will use the discussion to continue it.

    Cybercrime, cyberterrorism and cyber war

    Cybercrime is crime that uses computers or networks, or targets them. It ranges from fake invoices to stolen identities. The effects land on people: money lost, months of paperwork, fear, damaged trust, and sometimes delays to care for patients whose records are locked.

    Cyberterrorism and cyber war describe attacks on systems for political goals, or between countries. These are this course’s own plain definitions. People define them differently, and experts disagree about where the lines sit. So one of the discussion prompts asks you whether we are at cyber war now, and what you think “war” should mean.

    Goodman (2015) writes about how criminals use new technology. The publisher describes the book as a look at how criminals are often early adopters of new technology, with examples such as baby monitors, 3D printers and drones, and as a call for better security. It is not a legal guide. Use it as a prompt to think about the human effects of connected technology.

    Three trends

    • The Internet of Things (IoT) means everyday objects connected to the internet, such as doorbells, watches and baby monitors. Each one is another device to update, and another way in. A connected device nobody has listed is a device nobody is updating.
    • Big data means collecting huge amounts of information and finding patterns. The patterns can reveal things about you that you never chose to share, such as a health condition guessed from what you buy.
    • Quantum computing means a very different kind of computer. Experts warn that it could one day break some of today’s encryption. When, and how, is uncertain.

    Who is in charge online?

    The internet has no single owner. Governments make laws, and some filter or block parts of it. Platform companies set rules for what you can post and see. And you make choices of your own: settings, tools, and what you share. Where a law or a rule has changed what you can do or see online, you have felt this for yourself.

    Try it on Riverbend

    Both challenges are about identity theft. The first is about a volunteer at Riverbend Community Library, a made-up library, whose wallet is stolen away from the library. The second is about a message from Riverbend. Both cases are made up for this exercise and say nothing about how the library really works.

    Challenge

    Challenge: The stolen wallet (15 minutes)

    These are the eight steps, as cards. They are based on the Australian Signals Directorate’s page Recover from identity theft (2026), IDCARE’s website and the OAIC’s page on complaining to an organisation.

    Card Step
    A Contact your bank or card provider. Use the number on your card or the official app. Ask them to block, freeze or investigate suspicious activity
    B Secure your accounts. From a device you trust, change passwords, use a strong and unique password for each account, and turn on multi-factor authentication or passkeys
    C Contact IDCARE (https://www.idcare.org). A case manager can help you make a response plan
    D Check your credit. Ask a credit reporting body for a free credit report, dispute anything you do not recognise and consider a credit ban
    E Make a report through ReportCyber (https://www.cyber.gov.au/report-and-recover/report). If it was an online scam, report it to Scamwatch too. If your tax file number is involved, contact the Australian Taxation Office
    F Replace stolen identity documents. Follow your state or territory’s advice. For a passport, tell the Australian Passport Office. A Medicare card is replaced through Services Australia
    G Complain to the organisation that mishandled your information, then to the regulator. Complain to the organisation first. If it does not respond within a reasonable time (generally 30 days) or does not resolve it, you may complain to the regulator that covers it. Only relevant when an organisation’s handling of your information was part of the problem
    H Keep checking. Watch your accounts, mail and messages for unusual activity, because criminals may not use stolen details straight away

    Case A: the bus stop (made up). Mele volunteers at Riverbend on Saturdays. On her way home she puts her bag on a bench at the bus stop and turns to check the timetable. When she turns back, the bag is gone. It held her wallet, with her driver licence, her Medicare card and two bank cards. Within an hour her phone buzzes with a bank text: an online purchase of $480 that she did not make. The bag was taken from a public bench. Nobody, including Riverbend, has been said to have mishandled Mele’s information.

    1. Read the cards (3 minutes).
    2. Put the steps in order (12 minutes). List the cards you would use, in order, with one sentence for each saying why it goes there. Say which card or cards you would leave out, and why.

    One worked answer. Your order may differ and still be sound if you give a reason.

    Order Card Why it goes here
    1 A. Bank or card provider Money is leaving right now. The bank can block the cards and investigate the $480 charge
    2 B. Secure your accounts The thief holds her cards and documents, and may try to reach her online accounts. Strong passwords and multi-factor authentication make that harder
    3 C. IDCARE A case manager can help her make a plan. She has lost identity documents that could be used to open accounts
    4 D. Credit check A stolen licence and Medicare card could be used to apply for credit. A free credit report may show applications she did not make, and a credit ban may stop new ones
    5 E. ReportCyber A report puts the matter on record with the national system. It does not stop the money leaving, so it comes after the urgent steps
    6 F. Replace documents She needs new documents, but replacing them is less urgent than stopping the thief
    7 H. Keep checking The thief may not use the details straight away, so she should watch her accounts, mail and messages

    Left out: G. The bag was taken from a public bench, and no organisation has been said to have mishandled Mele’s information. Card G is only relevant when an organisation’s handling of the information was part of the problem. The case does not say Riverbend did anything wrong, so do not assume it.

    Accepted alternatives.

    • A and B can swap. A is the better start here because money is leaving, but a well-argued B first is accepted.
    • C and E can swap. IDCARE gives support and a plan. ReportCyber reports to the national system.
    • F can move earlier if you explain why she needs the document soon. It should not come before A.
    • H is not a one-off. Writing it as an ongoing step from the start is accepted.
    Challenge

    Challenge: A message from Riverbend (10 minutes)

    Use the cards and your answer from the previous challenge.

    Case B: the email (made up). Rhys is a Riverbend member. He receives an email from the library. It says that someone outside the library accessed its member database, and that his name, address, date of birth and phone number were included. A week later he receives a letter from a lender about a loan application he did not make, and he sees an unfamiliar enquiry on his credit report. The email does not say how the database was accessed.

    Say which cards are added or moved, and why. Use one or two sentences for each change. Remember that Riverbend is run by a council, so think about which regulator card G would point to.

    One worked answer.

    • G may be added. The email says someone accessed Riverbend’s database, but it does not say how, so do not assume the library was at fault. If Rhys thinks the library’s protection of his information was weak, he should complain to Riverbend first. If Riverbend does not respond or resolve it, he may complain to the regulator that covers it. The OAIC deals with complaints about organisations covered by the Privacy Act. A council-run library is generally covered by state or territory privacy law, so the right regulator may be a state or territory one, and the case does not say which state. If you add G, put it after the urgent steps, because it takes weeks. If you leave it out and give a reason, for example that the case does not show any fault, that is also accepted.
    • D moves up. The first signs are a loan application and a credit enquiry, so the credit check and a possible credit ban come earlier. He can dispute anything he does not recognise on the report.
    • A may change. The case mentions no suspicious bank transactions. He should still contact his bank or card provider if he is worried, but a learner who moves A later and gives a reason is accepted.
    • F may not apply. The case says only that his details were in the database. No documents are said to be stolen.
    • B, C, E and H stay sensible. Securing accounts, getting support, reporting and watching for later misuse all still fit.
    Callout

    Common mistakes

    • Starting with a report to a government service. Reporting matters, but it does not stop money leaving. Secure money and accounts first.
    • Assuming an organisation is at fault when the case does not say so. Card G only applies when an organisation’s handling of the information is part of the problem.
    • Complaining to a regulator first. The OAIC asks you to complain to the organisation before you complain to it.
    • Forgetting the step that never ends. Criminals may use stolen details months later, so keep checking.
    • Using a number or link from a message or caller. Use the number on your card, the official app, or a website you type in yourself.
    • Treating IDCARE as a police service or a regulator. It is Australia and New Zealand’s national identity and cyber support service. It helps you plan, but it does not make decisions about a complaint.
    • Not giving a reason. The reason shows you understand why the order matters.
    Challenge

    Quick check (5 minutes)

    1. Luca finds that a stolen licence was used to apply for a credit card in his name. The bank has cancelled the application. He wants to make it harder for anyone to open new credit in his name. Which step fits best?

      • A. Change the password on his email account and consider the problem dealt with.
      • B. Contact IDCARE and expect its case manager to withdraw the applications that were made in his name.
      • C. Make a report through ReportCyber and expect it to cancel the other applications automatically.
      • D. Request a free credit report from a credit reporting body and consider a credit ban.

    2. A supermarket’s loyalty app combines purchase records from millions of customers to guess which shoppers may have a health condition, and uses the guesses for targeted offers. Customers were never asked about their health. Which privacy concern is most direct?

      • A. Customers’ purchase records are not personal information, so no privacy concern arises.
      • B. The supermarket is not allowed to analyse purchase records without a customer’s written consent.
      • C. The offers might be irrelevant, which is a marketing problem and not a privacy one.
      • D. Patterns in big data can reveal sensitive details that customers never chose to share.

    3. A café installs a Wi-Fi security camera and leaves it on the password it came with. What is the main concern?

      • A. None, because a camera only watches and cannot be used to attack anyone.
      • B. It is another connected device that could be an easy way in, so it needs a changed password, updates and a place on the list of devices.
      • C. It is a concern only if the camera records sound.
      • D. It should be replaced every year, whatever its settings.
    1. D. A free credit report may show other applications, and a credit ban can make new credit harder to open. A password change does not touch credit, IDCARE helps with a plan but does not withdraw applications, and ReportCyber does not cancel them.
    2. D. Patterns in big data can reveal details that people never chose to share, such as a health condition. Option A is wrong because purchase records tied to a customer are personal information. Option B overstates the rule, and option C treats a privacy harm as a marketing detail.
    3. B. Connected devices are another way in, so each one needs a changed password, updates and a place on the list of devices someone looks after. A camera that connects to Wi-Fi can be attacked, and the concern does not depend on sound or on replacing it yearly.
    Discussion

    Reflect (5 minutes)

    Choose one prompt (or the one your instructor gives you) and write 3 to 6 sentences. Do not name other people or share private details such as passwords, card numbers or account details.

    Content note: the prompt about identity theft may be upsetting, for example if it has happened to you or someone close to you. You can answer it in general terms or choose another. IDCARE offers support, and it can help to talk to someone you trust.

    • Who is in charge online? Who do you think controls the internet, and where do you think the legal boundaries are? Think about governments, companies that run platforms, and your own choices. Where have you seen a law or a rule change what you can do or see online?
    • If it happened to you. Where would you go if you knew you had experienced identity theft? Who would you contact first, and who next? Which step would you find hardest, and why?
    • Are we at cyber war? Are we at cyber war now? There is no single agreed definition, so say what you think the word “war” should mean before you answer. What effect could attacks on systems have on ordinary people, such as people trying to get health care?
    • New technology and you. Choose one or two of these, and say what each could mean for your own life.
      • What are the implications of the Internet of Things (IoT), where everyday objects are connected to the internet?
      • How could big data affect you, for example through what companies could work out from what you buy or search?
      • What impact could quantum computing have, remembering that experts are unsure about when and how?

    Timing (55 minutes). Teaching text 20 minutes. Exercises 35 minutes: stolen wallet 15, message from Riverbend 10, quick check 5, discussion 5. The wider-world section is a light overview, so do not spend long on it in the teaching time. The discussion is where it gets airtime. Ask learners to read the Riverbend page before the session, or give 2 minutes at the start.

    Likely misconceptions.

    • Learners start with a report to a government service. Ask what stops the money leaving.
    • Learners assume an organisation was at fault in Case A or B. Ask which sentence in the case says so.
    • Learners treat IDCARE as police or a regulator.
    • Learners complain to a regulator before the organisation. Check the order on card G.
    • Learners say Riverbend’s regulator is “the OAIC” without thinking about the council. Ask who runs the library and which law that points to.
    • Learners treat “cyber war” as one agreed idea. Ask them to define “war” first.

    Content note. Identity theft is personal for some learners. Do not ask anyone for their own story. Let them do the exercise as pure ordering and skip the “why” sentences if they prefer. Keep IDCARE visible.

    Running the discussion. Use think-pair-share, with one prompt each for the pairs so that all the topics get covered. Give each pair a different prompt, then ask each pair for one sentence. For the cyber war prompt, ask pairs who disagree to swap definitions of “war”. For the new technology prompt, ask what each trend adds that the learner could change today, such as a router password.

    Tip. Write the eight card letters on cards or sticky notes and let pairs physically order them. Ask them to move a card when Case B is read out.

    Callout

    Go deeper

    • Australian Signals Directorate (2026) Recover from identity theft lists the steps and where to report.
    • IDCARE is Australia and New Zealand’s national identity and cyber support service.
    • Australian Signals Directorate (n.d.) Report is where to report cybercrime through ReportCyber.
    • Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (n.d.) Complain to an organisation or agency explains why you complain to the organisation first.
    Callout

    Want the credential?

    The Human Firewall microcredential covers Week 6 of this material and earns a digital badge.

    Key Points
    • In identity theft, stop the money first, secure your accounts, get support, check your credit, make a report, replace documents and keep checking.
    • A complaint comes after the urgent steps. Complain to the organisation first, then to the regulator that covers it, and only if the organisation’s handling was part of the problem.
    • Use the number on your card, the official app or a website you type in yourself, never a number or link from a message or caller.
    • Cybercrime lands on people, and experts disagree about where cyber war begins, so define your terms before you argue.
    • Connected devices, big data and quantum computing each change risk in a different way: another device to update, patterns you never chose to share, and a future threat to some encryption.
